metaTitle: Accounting Horizons Memorials Call for Nominations
title: Memorials
topics: Individuals whose work significantly advanced accounting thought
Individuals who revolutionized accounting practice and professional development

paragraphs: The Accounting Horizons Memorials Committee seeks nominations for memorials to be published in the journal, honoring deceased individuals who made significant contributions to accounting thought or practice. Nominees must have passed away at least 365 days before nomination.

Nominations should include a letter describing the nominee's contributions, three to five supporting letters, relevant primary source materials, and the nominee's vita or resume. All materials must be combined into a single PDF and submitted to memorials@aaahq.org.

metaTitle: Advancing Entrepreneurship Science with Meta-Analysis
title: Advancing Entrepreneurship Science with Meta-Analysis
topics: Meta-analytic approaches to entrepreneurship research
Systematic reviews of entrepreneurship literature
Quantitative synthesis of entrepreneurship findings
Methodological advances in meta-analysis applied to entrepreneurship
Integration and reconciliation of conflicting entrepreneurship research findings
Meta-analyses examining antecedents and consequences of entrepreneurial behavior
Comparative effectiveness of entrepreneurial interventions and strategies

paragraphs: This special issue seeks to advance entrepreneurship science through rigorous meta-analytic and systematic review methodologies. The call invites researchers to synthesize existing empirical findings in entrepreneurship, identifying patterns, contradictions, and knowledge gaps across the field. Meta-analyses can help consolidate fragmented research literatures and provide more robust conclusions about entrepreneurial phenomena.

The special issue is particularly interested in quantitative syntheses that examine both the drivers and outcomes of entrepreneurship, comparative assessments of different entrepreneurial approaches, and methodological innovations in applying meta-analytic techniques to entrepreneurship research. Contributions should leverage meta-analysis to advance theoretical understanding and practical knowledge in the entrepreneurship domain.

AI, big data and automation in project scheduling, forecasting, and resource allocation: Empirical or conceptual work on how intelligent systems are used to optimize project efficiency and adaptability.

Data-enabled project evaluation, benefits realisation, and impact assessment: Using data science to better measure and predict the value, outcomes, and sustainability of projects, including alignment with SDGs.

Theoretical and conceptual contributions linking data science and project studies: Frameworks and models that critically examine the intersection of data science and project management as evolving disciplines.

AI-empowered stakeholder engagement in large-scale or complex projects: Leveraging AI to enhance stakeholder analysis, communication, and collaboration in complex projects, optimizing engagement strategies and improving project outcomes through predictive insights and automated interaction tools.

paragraphs: This special issue examines how data science reshapes project, programme, and portfolio management practices. Rather than focusing on technical algorithmic details, it seeks to understand how managers can translate data and algorithmic insights into better decisions, governance, and value creation across the project lifecycle. The collection emphasizes managerial transformation rather than technology as an add-on.

Contributions should address how data-driven practices improve decision quality and accountability, how governance mechanisms adapt to data-intensive work, and how manager and team competencies evolve. The special issue particularly welcomes research on adoption conditions, implementation challenges, and safeguards for ethical use, bias mitigation, and transparency in decision-making.

Submissions should prioritize actionable insights for practitioners through conceptual frameworks, empirical case studies, and practical artifacts such as decision frameworks, governance templates, and maturity models. Cross-sector studies demonstrating tangible managerial outcomes and connections to organizational strategy and broader societal value are especially encouraged.

metaTitle: ​Assessing the Value and Impact of Digital Transformation in the Built Environment
title: Assessing the Value and Impact of Digital Transformation in the Built Environment
topics: How the value of digital technologies is conceptualized and measured
Opportunities and challenges related to value creation for individuals, organizations, and wider systems
Adoption and usability of digital technologies
Economic, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) implications of digital technologies
Measurable effects (both positive and negative) of digitalization in the built environment

paragraphs: Despite widespread digitalization efforts in the built environment sector, practitioners remain uncertain about the value of digital investments, viewing them as risky ventures with unclear returns and ambiguous benefits. This special issue seeks to address the insufficient understanding of how digital transformation creates value across the sector by establishing frameworks and gathering evidence on the impact of digital technologies.

The issue welcomes contributions from multiple disciplines examining how value is understood, measured, and realized through digital adoption. Contributions may assess value quantitatively through efficiency metrics and financial indicators, or qualitatively through improvements in work practices, sustainability, and service quality. The editors invite case studies, comparative analyses, methodological frameworks, and empirical evaluations offering both qualitative and quantitative perspectives on digital technologies in the built environment.

metaTitle: Benchmarking Adaptive Supply Chains: Performance Metrics, Maturity Models, and Socio-Technical Configurations
title: Benchmarking Adaptive Supply Chains: Performance Metrics, Maturity Models, and Socio-Technical Configurations
topics: Benchmarking adaptive supply chain performance across industries and regions
Performance metrics and composite indices for adaptive, sustainable, and resilient supply chains
Supply chain maturity models and benchmarking trajectories
Socio-technical configurations and comparative performance outcomes
Benchmarking digital and AI-enabled supply chain systems
Performance frontiers and efficiency analysis of adaptive supply chains
Cross-country and institutional benchmarking of supply chain adaptability
Governance, collaboration, and coordination as benchmarked performance drivers
Comparative analysis of sustainability and resilience performance trade-offs

paragraphs: Organizations face ongoing disruptions and must adapt their supply chains while managing sustainability and digital transformation. However, there is limited frameworks for measuring and comparing adaptive supply chain performance across different organizations and contexts. This special issue seeks to advance research that uses benchmarking logic to systematically evaluate how well supply chains adapt.

The special issue emphasizes understanding adaptive performance through the interaction of people, technology, governance, and sustainability practices. Rather than treating adaptation as a general concept, research should operationalize adaptability with measurable constructs and benchmarking frameworks that highlight performance differences between configurations.

Contributions should employ rigorous comparative designs using quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods to benchmark adaptive supply chains across industries and countries. By identifying which configurations perform better and under what conditions, the research will provide actionable insights for practitioners and policymakers.

journal: Journal of Organizational Effectiveness: People and Performance
metaTitle: Beyond AI Adoption: People Management, Work Design and Sustainable Performance in AI-Enabled Organisations
title: Beyond AI Adoption: People Management, Work Design and Sustainable Performance in AI-Enabled Organisations
topics: AI-enabled recruitment, selection and fair access to work: How AI screening, automated assessments, candidate ranking, video interviews and people analytics affect fairness, validity, transparency, accessibility and selection outcomes.

AI-supported training, development and capability building: How AI-enabled learning systems, skills analytics, career platforms and talent systems affect reskilling, development access, career visibility and employee capability.

AI-enabled performance management, monitoring and evaluation: How algorithmic monitoring, datafication and AI-supported appraisal affect fairness, trust, employee agency, wellbeing, reasonable adjustment and performance outcomes.

Work design, job quality and employee voice in AI-enabled workplaces: How AI changes autonomy, workload, coordination, meaningful work, participation, consultation and human oversight in people-management decisions.

Inclusion, disability, governance and sustainable organisational effectiveness: How organisations design AI-enabled HRM systems that reduce bias, support EDI, protect disabled workers and applicants, strengthen trust and contribute to sustainable organisational performance.

paragraphs: AI systems are increasingly used in HR functions such as recruitment, employee analytics, training, performance management and workforce planning. While organizations often expect these systems to improve efficiency and fairness, they raise concerns about transparency, employee wellbeing, job quality and whether such systems genuinely enhance organizational performance. This special issue shifts focus from simply whether organizations adopt AI to how AI-enabled HR systems should be designed, governed and experienced to benefit employees and organizational effectiveness.

The special issue examines the relationship between AI-enabled HR practices and sustainable organizational performance, considering both potential benefits and risks. It invites research exploring when and how AI strengthens or undermines work quality, fairness, employee voice, inclusion and capability development. The collection addresses emerging regulatory interest from bodies like the OECD and EU AI Act, which recognize that AI in employment decisions requires responsible governance.

Contributions may address AI in recruitment, training and development, performance management, work design, employee voice, inclusion and governance. The special issue seeks conceptual, empirical and methodological work that is theoretically rigorous, grounded in evidence and relevant to practitioners seeking to implement AI responsibly while supporting human capability and sustainable performance.

metaTitle: Beyond Black and White - Shades of Grey Leadership​
title: Beyond Black and White – Shades of Grey Leadership
topics: Conceptual development of grey leadership
Perspectives on grey leadership
What is grey leadership?
Types of grey leadership: constructing the continuum
How do we better understand grey leadership as a construct
Novel insights
Grey leadership practices
How does grey leadership materialize in the workplace?
What are the implications for followers and/or leaders?
What are the implications for organizations and/or society?
Can grey leadership ever be good for an organization?
What is the role of context in the enactment of grey leadership?
Case studies of grey leadership
Leading in the shadows
The ambiguities of grey leadership
Are there any benefits to leading in the shadows?
The role of HR in grey leadership
Understanding the continuum from grey to black/bad leadership practices
How does grey leadership differ if at all from black leadership?
Is grey leadership dark leadership in disguise
Dealing with grey leadership
How to combat grey leadership?
How to prevent it from becoming black/bad?

paragraphs: This special issue examines grey leadership, a phenomenon occupying the spectrum between constructive and destructive leadership practices. Grey leadership encompasses ambiguous and contested behaviors that are neither clearly beneficial nor overtly harmful—such as subtle rule-bending, enabling harmful dynamics through inaction, or normalizing problematic conduct. These behaviors often escape clear moral judgment or legal consequences yet significantly impact organizational relationships and culture.

The concept integrates ethical, emotional, and contextual dimensions of leadership by recognizing mixed moral intent, inconsistent values signaling, and situationally contingent consequences. Grey leadership serves as a conceptual bridge across fragmented leadership literatures, revealing how contradictions in intent, signals, and outcomes interact dynamically within specific contexts and are negotiated through relational processes.

The special issue invites theoretical, empirical, and case-based contributions exploring how grey leadership is enacted, sustained, challenged, or normalized in organizations. It seeks to clarify the continuum from grey to darker leadership practices and develop context-sensitive approaches for understanding leadership ambiguities in complex organizational environments.

metaTitle: Career Development and Student Entrepreneurship for University-to-Work Transition in Emerging Economies
title: Career Development and Student Entrepreneurship for University-to-Work Transition in Emerging Economies
topics: Student Entrepreneurial Activities as a Pathway to University-to-Work Transition: exploring how students' engagement in small and micro-businesses might facilitate or hinder their transition into the labour market

Career Development and Employability Skills Acquisition: exploring how students' entrepreneurial engagement contributes to or hinders the development of essential employability skills and career readiness

Institutional and Contextual Factors in Emerging Economies: exploring how factors such as institutional support, government policies, culture and economic conditions shape student entrepreneurship and university-to-work transition outcomes
Cross-regional Comparative Insights & Theoretical Advancement: examining comparative perspectives on how student entrepreneurship affects university-to-work transition in different regions

Inner Development Goals and the Human Dimension of Entrepreneurship: integration of the IDGuide into entrepreneurship and business education, and how cognitive, social, and self-leadership competencies promote entrepreneurial behaviour and employability among students

paragraphs: This special issue seeks empirical research on how student entrepreneurship influences the transition from university education to employment in emerging economies. The focus is on understanding how entrepreneurial experiences during higher education contribute to career development, employability skills, and readiness for labour market entry.

The call addresses a gap in research regarding student entrepreneurship's role in university-to-work transition, despite evidence that entrepreneurial activities provide experiential learning opportunities for developing workplace skills. The special issue aims to inform policymakers, university administrators, and industry experts about improving graduate employment outcomes while contributing to United Nations Sustainable Development Goals related to quality education, decent work, and reduced inequalities.

The special issue welcomes qualitative, quantitative (longitudinal designs only), and mixed methods studies. Submissions should prioritize career development literature and address how student entrepreneurship affects career pathways, skills development, institutional support systems, and labour market entry in emerging economies and developing regions.

metaTitle: China and Fragile Countries: Investment, Initiatives, and Impact?
title: China and Fragile Countries: Investment, Initiatives, and Impact
topics: Contexts: What are the types of contexts where Chinese organizations are active in social investments and initiatives for development and peace?

Strategies and modes: How do Chinese enterprises, including State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and Privately-Owned Enterprises (POEs), function as agents of development, peace and stability? How do the strategies and activities of Chinese POEs differ compared to SOEs as far as these activities are concerned?
Collaborations and alliances: How do Chinese enterprises collaborate with non-Chinese organizations in fragile settings?

Links to IGOs: How does China interact with Inter-Governmental Organizations (IGOs), such as the UN Peacebuilding Commission (PBC), Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA), and Department of Peace Operations (DPO)? What role do IGOs play in facilitating social investment and initiatives by Chinese enterprises?

Contrasts to Western models: To what extent do the actions and impact of Chinese organizations in fragile settings necessitate a redefinition of development initiative, and how does its meaning differ compared to Western notions, such as that of 'liberal peace'?

Local and hybrid models: Beyond the "liberal vs. developmental" paradigms comparison, how do Chinese practices in fragile settings interact with existing international and local frameworks? Are we witnessing the emergence of hybrid models in countries where both Chinese and Western countries are active?

paragraphs: This special issue examines China's multifaceted engagement in fragile countries characterized by weak institutions, limited state capacity, and insecurity. The focus encompasses Chinese foreign direct investment, corporate initiatives, and government-level activities aimed at development and peacebuilding, from the "Going Out" period through the Belt and Road Initiative era to present-day involvement in conflict mediation and UN peacekeeping operations.

The collection seeks to advance understanding of how Chinese actors—including state-owned and privately-owned enterprises as well as government agencies—approach development and peace in fragile settings. Particular attention is given to the environmental and social impacts of these initiatives, how they differ from Western approaches, and how they interact with existing international frameworks and local contexts.

The special issue welcomes both empirical and conceptual contributions examining the strategies, collaborations, and effectiveness of Chinese organizations in fragile countries, including their relationships with inter-governmental organizations and the emergence of hybrid models where Chinese and Western actors operate simultaneously.

metaTitle: Circular and Future-Adaptive Facilities
title: Circular and Future-Adaptive Facilities
topics: Redefining building performance and lifecycle value through Facilities Management
Digital transformation in Facilities Management
Integrating climate resilience and future-adaptive strategies in FM
Sustainable building operations and innovations in energy efficiency
Integrated safety, risk, waste, and emission management for total wellbeing

paragraphs: Facilities Management is being repositioned as a strategic discipline to address the built environment's challenges stemming from climate change, technological disruption, and resource scarcity. This special issue seeks scholarly contributions exploring how FM can enable transitions toward resilient, efficient, and adaptable infrastructure while integrating circularity, digital tools, and future-oriented management practices.

The call invites research on lifecycle value optimization, digital innovations like BIM and digital twins, climate resilience strategies, sustainable operations, energy efficiency, safety management, and occupant wellbeing. Contributions may encompass empirical research, conceptual studies, or industry case analyses examining how FM professionals can translate technological advances and circular principles into practical, scalable solutions.

The special issue, developed alongside the Facilities Management Futures 2026 Conference, aims to advance both theoretical understanding and applied practice while contributing to broader goals including sustainable communities, responsible production, climate action, and improved occupant wellbeing.

metaTitle: Crafting Shape in a Fluid World - The Intersection of Marketing and External Forces
title: Crafting Shape in a Fluid World – The Intersection of Marketing and External Forces
topics: Consumer responses to global disruptions (e.g., inflation, supply chain fragility, climate events, tariffs, war)
Impact of AI, automation, and platform-based ecosystems on consumer well-being and happiness
How to enhance responsible consumption (e.g., reducing food waste and increasing adoptions of green energy and public transportation)
How to serve marginalized and disadvantaged consumers and enhance equality among gender, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status through marketing and equitable practices
Evolving consumer purchase patterns and consumption practices around brand ethics, transparency, and sustainability
How firms can navigate sociopolitical activism (e.g., Should brands take a stand or remain silent?)
Recalibrating brand-consumer relationships in times of social and political polarization
Cross-cultural and cross-generational consumer insights in a post-globalization era
Retail innovation in response to external forces, trends, disruptions, and shifting consumer expectations
Marketing strategies for enhancing trust, loyalty, engagement in uncertain environments

paragraphs: Marketing practice is being transformed by technological advances, geopolitical shifts, economic pressures, and growing demands for sustainability and social responsibility. Retail environments serve as key sites where these transformations unfold, with both physical and digital channels becoming laboratories for new consumer engagement and adaptive strategies. Consumers now demand greater brand ethics, transparency, and societal contributions, while external disruptions like supply chain fragility, inflation, and geopolitical tensions reshape pricing and sourcing. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence and platform ecosystems are fundamentally changing how consumers access information and make purchase decisions.

This special issue invites scholars to explore how consumer behavior intersects with external forces in today's fluid world. The call welcomes conceptual and empirical research that advances theory while providing practical insights for managers facing these complexities. Particular attention is given to the retail sector as a focal context for understanding these dynamics, including how firms can maintain agility and personalization while managing operational challenges in uncertain environments.

title: Critical Dimensions of the Global Energy Transition
topics: Fossil Low Carbon Structural Shift in Energy Sector
Future Agenda & Bibliometric Reviews on Energy Transition
Energy Asset Prioritization & Modernization for Energy Development
Technological Innovation in Renewables For Future Energy Markets
Solutions to Bottlenecks for Sustainable Energy Efficiency Models

Future and Emerging Models of Circular Economy & Waste Management
Corporate Energy Practice Attraction: Board Level Decision, Policy Dilemmas & Geopolitics
Leadership, Gender & Human Capital

paragraphs: This special issue examines the global energy transition from fossil fuels to low-carbon technologies, addressing the systemic transformation required to mitigate climate change and achieve sustainable development. The call seeks applied, problem-solving research that explores the interplay between technological innovation, policy frameworks, market dynamics, and geopolitical factors across different geographical contexts.

The special issue welcomes contributions on energy sector management, simulation tools, circular economy approaches, and integrated models that assess economic and environmental pathways. Research should address challenges such as green finance, supply chain resilience, carbon neutrality, and policy mechanisms for successful energy transitions, as well as emerging topics including leadership development, gender issues, and professional training in the energy sector.

metaTitle: Developing Management Capability in Sustainability Leadership
title: Developing Management Capability in Sustainability Leadership
topics: Sustainability leadership capability development for managers as a force for positive change and compassionate flourishing
Anthropocentric assumptions limiting leaders' engagement with planetary health and multi-species justice
Systematic and systemic application of sustainability leadership capability development for resolving complex and disruptive challenges
Personal values and morals as drivers of managers' sustainability leadership behaviors, decisions and actions
Benevolent influence through individual and collective agency in sustainability leadership development

paragraphs: This special issue seeks interdisciplinary research exploring how managers can develop sustainability leadership capacity across interconnected levels. The focus spans macro outcomes related to compassionate flourishing and planetary health, meso-level organizational and community goals, and micro-level personal values and behavioral inputs of managers. The issue aims to identify connection points in the entire sustainability leadership development system.

Through contributions from diverse scholars, the special issue will examine how sustainability leadership capability can serve as a positive force in addressing global challenges, how it can be applied systematically within organizations and communities, and how managers' personal values and morals translate into sustainable behaviors and decisions. Recommendations emerging from the issue are intended to benefit academics, practitioners, and broader environmental outcomes.

journal: Qualitative Research in Organizations and Management
metaTitle: Doing Entrepreneurship at the Margins: Qualitative Insights
title: Doing Entrepreneurship at the Margins: Qualitative Insights
topics: Entrepreneurship as organizing under conditions of marginalization
Lived experience and everyday practices of entrepreneurs at the margins
Marginality as an analytical lens for qualitative theory-building
Power, inequality, and access in entrepreneurial organizing
Informal, community-based, and non-market entrepreneurial activity
Gendered, racialized, Indigenous, and migrant entrepreneurship
Entrepreneurship in Global South and under-researched contexts
Legitimacy, stigma, and boundary work in marginalized entrepreneurship
Resourcefulness, bricolage, and survival strategies under constraint
Care, affect, ethics, and relational practices in entrepreneurial organizing
Methodological challenges and innovations in researching entrepreneurship in marginalized populations

paragraphs: While quantitative, positivist approaches have traditionally dominated entrepreneurship research, they often fail to capture the lived experiences of marginalized entrepreneurs who remain underrepresented in scholarship despite their significant contributions to local economies. Qualitative research is better suited to exploring the meanings, practices, and organizing processes that hypothesis-driven designs typically obscure.

This special issue invites qualitative research that examines entrepreneurship at the margins as a site for theory-building. The focus encompasses marginalized entrepreneurs across gender, race, migration, disability, age, and Indigenous contexts, particularly in Global South settings where research access challenges are compounded by institutional barriers and epistemic dominance of Global North perspectives.

Contributions should treat marginality as an analytical lens rather than merely a research setting, bringing together reflexive scholarship that advances cumulative qualitative understanding of entrepreneurship as organizing while exploring core themes of power, inequality, agency, legitimacy, and meaning-making.

metaTitle: Financial inclusion strategies, technology, and risk management: emerging trends and global perspectives
title: Financial inclusion strategies, technology, and risk management: emerging trends and global perspectives
topics: The use of satellite and alternative data in financial risk assessment
Financial technologies, artificial intelligence, and emerging risks
Technological, modelling, and cybersecurity risks in the financial system
Sustainable finance, capital allocation, and systemic risk
Financial inclusion, digitalisation, and resilience to economic shocks
Decentralised finance (DeFi) and risks to financial stability
Regenerative finance (ReFi) and long-term risk management
Blockchain, tokenisation, and traceability in sustainability and green finance projects
Regulatory and supervisory frameworks for sustainable finance, fintech, decentralised finance (DeFi), and regenerative finance (ReFi)
Applications of big data, artificial intelligence, and machine learning in sustainable finance
Supervision, regulation, and macroprudential policies in response to emerging risks

paragraphs: Financial systems face evolving risks from climate change, digitalisation, and new financial ecosystems that challenge existing supervision and policy frameworks. Advanced technologies like artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and satellite systems enhance risk identification and monitoring, yet introduce new technological and cybersecurity threats. Sustainable finance and financial inclusion have emerged as instruments for managing long-term risks and strengthening financial system resilience, though questions persist regarding data quality and greenwashing.

This special issue seeks theoretical and empirical research examining the challenges and opportunities arising from the convergence of technology, sustainability, and financial inclusion. Contributions should adopt financial and risk management perspectives, with particular interest in studies addressing implications for financial stability, prudential supervision, and public policy design.

metaTitle: From theory to impact - how do organizations benefit from systems research?​
title: From theory to impact – how do organizations benefit from systems research?
topics: Leading change in dynamic societies through complex-adaptive systems models
Structure, practice, and impact of educational systems on employment, income, social transformation
Added value of AI, blockchain, and other technical implementations of systems operations
Effects of systems-oriented consulting services
Limitations of systems designs and interplay with improvisation and heuristics
Leadership systems development, application, and assessment
Cultural differences and specificities affecting the application of formal systems models

paragraphs: This special issue seeks research demonstrating how organizations apply systems theory and cybernetics to create tangible impact. Rather than focusing solely on theoretical development, the issue invites contributions showing practical benefits across management, education, engineering, and other domains where formal systems approaches are relevant. Diverse article types are welcomed, including case studies, practitioner papers, viewpoints, and technical reports, allowing authors to present their work in varied formats while maintaining clear arguments supported by suitable evidence.

The special issue addresses academia's responsibility to engage with grand societal challenges and sustainable development goals. Systems theory and cybernetics offer tools for understanding complex dynamics beyond simplistic solutions, enabling more comprehensive approaches to contemporary problems. Submissions examining applications in the Global South and Eastern Hemisphere, particularly those providing firsthand evidence of systems research's effectiveness in these contexts, are especially encouraged.

metaTitle: Green HRM in the Global South: Establishing Sustainability, Responsible Transformations, and Resilient Organizational Development
title: Green HRM in the Global South: Establishing Sustainability, Responsible Transformations, and Resilient Organizational Development
topics: Contextualizing GHRM in the Global South (i.e. the adoption of GHRM, implementation barriers, contribution to sustainability)
GHRM and work outcomes in the Global South (i.e. the effect of GHRM on green and non-green individual and organizational outcomes)
How GHRM can enhance staff well-being in informal staffing settings (i.e. the relationship between GHRM and workplace happiness, job security, and inclusive practices of staffing, etc.)
GHRM in sector-specific context in the Global South (i.e. manufacturing, IT, higher education, hospitality, etc.)
National perspectives of GHRM in the Global South (i.e. how GHRM can facilitate effective economic transitions given the frequent scarcity of the resources and climate vulnerability)
Leadership, organizational culture, management commitment to sustainable practices (how the aforementioned factors can shape GHRM practices in contexts where pro-environmental values may be nascent)

GHRM and Organizational Resilience in the Global South (i.e. why and how GHRM can serve as a tool that contributes to organizational resilience in the light of environmental and operational disruptions)
The role of AI and digital transformation in enabling GHRM in the Global South
Success stories and case studies of organizations that pioneered the implementation of GHRM in the Global South

paragraphs: Green HRM (GHRM) integrates environmental responsibility into HR practices and procedures, enabling organizations to achieve sustainability goals while transforming employees into sustainability advocates. However, most GHRM research originates from the Global North, leaving implementation in the Global South—Latin America, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East—insufficiently studied and scattered across specific contexts.

This gap in scholarship risks producing GHRM frameworks disconnected from the socioeconomic and institutional realities of Global South countries. The special issue seeks to address this by inviting conceptual papers, empirical research, and scholarly discussions that examine how GHRM can advance sustainability, social justice, and economic stability in resource-constrained environments while exploring the unique obstacles and opportunities for GHRM adoption in Global South organizations.

journal: Journal of Service Theory and Practice
metaTitle: Immersive Technologies and Sensory Service Experiences: Redefining the Customer Journey and Value Creation in the Age of AI
title: Immersive Technologies and Sensory Service Experiences: Redefining the Customer Journey and Value Creation in the Age of AI
topics: Sensory-enabled immersive service experiences across the customer journey
Multisensory cue interaction and cross-modal congruence in immersive services
Role of immersive technologies, including VR, AR, and MR, as strategic service touchpoints
AI-enabled adaptation, personalization, and orchestration of multisensory stimuli
Generative AI and learning systems in immersive service design and delivery
Customer perceptions, emotions, intentions, and real behaviors in immersive services
Value creation and value co-creation through multisensory immersive services

paragraphs: This special issue examines how immersive technologies like virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality are transforming service experiences by enabling multisensory digital environments. The focus is on understanding how visual, auditory, haptic, olfactory, and gustatory cues interact within these environments to shape customer perception and behavior across different stages of the customer journey.

Research on sensory marketing demonstrates that consumers process sensory information through cross-modal interactions rather than in isolation. While immersive technologies hold significant potential for creating rich multisensory experiences, existing research has primarily focused on audio-visual features, leaving a gap in understanding how diverse sensory stimuli collectively influence customer perceptions and value creation throughout their journey.

The special issue aims to advance service theory by investigating immersive experiences as interconnected touchpoints that reshape customer journeys. It welcomes research exploring how artificial intelligence can augment and personalize multisensory experiences, and invites critical examination of existing theoretical and methodological approaches in service research.

metaTitle: Industry 5.0-driven Product Lifecycle Management: toward human-centric, sustainable, and resilient manufacturing
title: Industry 5.0-driven Product Lifecycle Management: toward human-centric, sustainable, and resilient manufacturing
topics: Redesigning PLM Systems for Industry 5.0
Human-Centric PLM and Operator Development
Circular Economy Integration within PLM
Sustainable Lifecycle Assessment and Net-Zero Strategies
Resilient Manufacturing and Adaptive Lifecycle Management
Governance, Interoperability, and Data Management Frameworks
Decision-Support and Managerial Transformation
Sector-Specific Applications with Cross-Industry Implications

paragraphs: This special issue addresses how Product Lifecycle Management systems must evolve to support Industry 5.0's three foundational principles: human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience. Traditional PLM systems, designed primarily for data integration and process efficiency, lack mechanisms to support operator well-being, embed circular economy strategies, ensure regulatory compliance, or enable rapid adaptation during disruptions.

The special issue introduces PLM 5.0 as a strategic governance platform that integrates lifecycle data, human interaction, sustainability metrics, and adaptive decision-making across industrial ecosystems. It seeks conceptual, empirical, methodological, and case-based contributions that explore how PLM systems should be redesigned, how organizations can integrate circular economy principles, what governance frameworks are needed, and how manufacturing can build resilience through lifecycle management.

The call is addressed to an international research community in PLM, manufacturing management, circular economy, and industrial sustainability, aiming to advance both theoretical understanding and practical guidance for enterprises transitioning toward more responsible and adaptive lifecycle management practices.

journal: International Journal of Web Information Systems
metaTitle: Knowledge-enhanced Large Language Models for Web Information Systems in Health and Education
title: Knowledge-enhanced Large Language Models for Web Information Systems in Health and Education
topics: Knowledge-enhanced LLM architectures for Web information systems
Knowledge graphs, ontologies, and Web semantics for LLM reasoning and generation
Retrieval-augmented generation for Web-based health and education services
Web knowledge mining, information extraction, and knowledge integration for LLM-based systems
Multimodal knowledge representation and fusion for health and learning applications on the Web
Trustworthy, explainable, and privacy-preserving LLMs for sensitive Web environments
LLM-enhanced medical information retrieval, health question answering, and decision support
LLM-enhanced personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, and learning feedback
Agentic LLMs and AI agents for Web-based health and education service management
Benchmarks, datasets, evaluation metrics, and real-world applications of knowledge-enhanced LLMs in Web information systems

paragraphs: Healthcare and education systems increasingly rely on complex, knowledge-intensive web platforms generating large-scale heterogeneous data. While Large Language Models excel at natural language understanding and human-computer interaction, directly applying general-purpose LLMs to these domains faces significant challenges including factual accuracy, lack of domain knowledge representation, and insufficient interpretability needed for sensitive applications.

Knowledge-enhanced LLMs address these limitations by incorporating structured knowledge, Web semantics, and multimodal representations into language models. This approach improves reliability, explainability, and controllability while enabling better integration with existing system components such as data retrieval and information management modules. The special issue seeks high-quality research on theoretical models, methods, frameworks, and applications of knowledge-enhanced LLMs specifically designed for healthcare and education web services.

metaTitle: Leadership and Governance in Complex Learning Systems: Risk, Knowledge and Entrepreneurship
title: Leadership and Governance in Complex Learning Systems: Risk, Knowledge and Entrepreneurship
topics: Leadership and governance as systemic architectures of observation, decision and learning
Enterprise-wide risk management, knowledge management and entrepreneurship as interconnected cybernetic processes
Cross-sector analyses of universities, health systems, research institutes, public agencies and professional service firms as complex learning systems
Reflexive and second-order perspectives on how organisations construct and revise their own governance arrangements
Theory-as-method applications using cybernetics, systems thinking or complexity frameworks

paragraphs: Knowledge-intensive organisations face mounting complexity from resource constraints, digitalisation, accountability demands, and geopolitical pressures. Existing research on these challenges remains fragmented across disciplinary silos and often lacks systemic understanding of how these institutions observe, interpret and respond to complexity.

This special issue integrates typically isolated scholarly conversations about leadership, governance, risk, knowledge and entrepreneurship within a cybernetic framework. It explores the interconnected processes of observation, communication, decision and learning that enable organisations to adapt and remain viable across sectors including universities, health systems, research institutes and public agencies.

The special issue emphasises reflexive inquiry into how leadership systems observe themselves and how learning architectures evolve. Using cybernetic and systems thinking as analytical approaches rather than metaphors, it aims to demonstrate their continued relevance for understanding contemporary organisational phenomena and addressing major societal challenges related to health, education, innovation, sustainability and democratic governance.

journal: Journal of Enterprising Communities: People and Places in the Global Economy
metaTitle: Lifestyle Entrepreneurship: Challenges, Innovations, and Community Impact
title: Lifestyle Entrepreneurship: Challenges, Innovations, and Community Impact
topics: Profile of lifestyle entrepreneurs: sociodemographic characteristics, values and experiences

Motivations for lifestyle entrepreneurship: sense of belonging (roots) to the territory, maintaining the culture and traditions of the territory, quality of life, self-fulfillment, balance between personal and professional life
Contextual factors: impact of social networks, public policies, local entrepreneurial ecosystems and socioeconomic environment
Challenges faced: financial instability, lack of institutional support, technological and market barriers, lack of qualified human resources
Impact of lifestyle entrepreneurship on local development: job creation, stimulation of the circular economy and contribution to sustainability
Resilience and adaptation strategies: innovative and sustainable solutions adopted by entrepreneurs in territories
Comparative case studies between different regions and sectors

paragraphs: Lifestyle entrepreneurship represents a growing but fragmented research area that extends beyond traditional profit-maximization approaches to encompass quality of life, personal fulfillment, and work-life balance. These entrepreneurs prioritize autonomy and alignment with personal values while establishing ventures often in tourism, hospitality, crafts, and creative sectors, frequently in rural or low-density areas where they contribute to local economic development and cultural preservation.

Despite increasing recognition of its significance, existing research lacks an integrated perspective examining both entrepreneur characteristics and their operational ecosystems. Lifestyle entrepreneurs face persistent challenges including financial instability, seasonal market dependence, and insufficient institutional support, while contextual factors such as social networks, public policies, and cultural influences significantly shape their business structures and community interactions.

This special issue seeks submissions examining the multifaceted dimensions of lifestyle entrepreneurship, from entrepreneur profiles and motivations to the strategies they employ for resilience and sustainability. Research should address how these ventures impact local development and explore the role of innovation and formal and informal networks in ensuring long-term project viability across different regions and sectors.

metaTitle: Management in Emerging, Developing, and Transition Economies: Context, Mechanisms, and Outcomes
title: Management in Emerging, Developing, and Transition Economies: Context, Mechanisms, and Outcomes
topics: How and with what consequences do firms substitute private or community governance for missing or unreliable formal institutions, and which mechanisms make these substitutes durable or fragile?

Which configurations of resources, networks, and legitimacy enable opportunity discovery and scaling in thin or nascent markets, and how do founders and top managers navigate uncertainty and institutional gaps across growth stages?

Under resource constraints and uneven enforcement, what capability bundles allow firms to align environmental initiatives with competitive outcomes, and how do local cultural or state priorities shape these trajectories?
How do reporting, budgeting, and control systems adapt when enforcement is uneven, and what are the implications for investment, innovation, market signals, and stakeholder trust in emerging markets?

How do contextual communication and power structures condition the effectiveness of leadership, employee voice, engagement, and performance systems in transition settings, and what are the boundary conditions for transferability?
How do commitments to learning and open innovation translate into performance when institutions are in flux, and which organisational routines, such as bricolage, mediate these effects?

How do political ties, state ownership, or party networks shape strategic decision-making, board dynamics, and accountability in firms and hybrid organisations operating under volatile or contested regulatory regimes?
How do gender, ethnicity, and other social cleavages intersect with institutional voids to shape leadership careers, informal influence, and patterns of inclusion and exclusion inside organisations?

In conflict-affected, fragile, or post-disaster settings, which leadership practices and governance arrangements enable organisational resilience, continuity of services, and recovery, and what trade-offs do they imply?

How do regional, cross-border, or diaspora networks among managers, professionals, and researchers mediate the transfer, translation, and contestation of management ideas and leadership models across institutional contexts?

paragraphs: Most management research has been developed in Western contexts, leaving significant gaps in understanding leadership and organizational practices in emerging, developing, and transition economies—regions that now generate nearly half of global economic output. These economies operate under distinct institutional conditions where formal institutions are incomplete or unevenly enforced, requiring firms to rely on alternative coordination mechanisms and making context a primary determinant of business strategy and performance.

This special issue addresses this literature gap by centering emerging, developing, and transition economies as objects of theoretical inquiry rather than control variables. It invites studies across governance, entrepreneurship, sustainability, and leadership that examine how management practices evolve, adapt, or are translated when formal rules and infrastructures cannot be taken for granted. The call welcomes quantitative surveys, experiments, qualitative ethnographies, mixed-methods research, and conceptual work, particularly comparative studies spanning regions or contrasting different institutional settings.

metaTitle: Meaning, Meaningfulness, and Purpose at Work: Towards Conceptual Clarity and Integration
title: Meaning, Meaningfulness, and Purpose at Work: Towards Conceptual Clarity and Integration
topics: Authenticity and alignment of work with personal values

Sustaining purpose and meaning over time
Meaning of work
Meaningful work
Purpose of work
Decent work
Sustainable Careers

paragraphs: This special issue addresses the interconnected but conceptually distinct notions of meaning, meaningfulness, and purpose in work contexts. While meaning relates to personal interpretations and values alignment, meaningfulness encompasses the emotional and experiential aspects of work fulfillment, and purpose refers to long-term direction and self-transcendent goals. The special issue seeks to clarify these constructs and their relationships to advance theoretical understanding of human fulfillment at work.

The collection welcomes empirical and theoretical research examining how workers assign meaning to their roles, experience fulfillment through work, and pursue purposeful careers. The focus extends across diverse occupational contexts and considers how meaning and purpose sustain over time and interact with broader life considerations, technological change, and the concept of decent work.

metaTitle: Nordic Consumer Culture​

Contradictions in Nordic consumer culture

paragraphs: The Nordic region exhibits a distinctive consumer culture marked by paradoxes: societies balance egalitarian values with status-consciousness, individualism with collective welfare systems, and modesty with aspiration. The Nordic welfare state uniquely aligns state and individual interests, creating a distinctive marketplace. Despite growing research examining Nordic consumption patterns—from branding and cultural phenomena to alternative food markets and immigrant experiences—significant gaps remain in understanding how these contradictions manifest across consumption practices and market formations.

This special issue seeks to advance comprehensive scholarship on Nordic consumer culture by publishing novel and critically grounded research that explores the interplay between state, market, and consumer practices. The editors welcome contributions analyzing market dynamics, investigating paradoxes inherent in Nordic consumption, and examining how macro-level contexts including welfare policies, cultural myths, and political ideologies shape consumer behavior, with particular interest in innovative methodologies and interdisciplinary approaches.

metaTitle: Observing Intimacies: System-Theoretical Analyses of Love Relationships Today

Gender

Queer intimacies and inclusion/exclusion effects

paragraphs: Intimate relationships have undergone significant transformations globally, with relationship ideals and forms becoming increasingly diverse across commitment types, duration, and organization. This special issue aims to advance knowledge production by promoting observational rather than normative approaches to intimacies, encouraging data-driven scholarship that moves beyond polarized public debates about relationships.

The issue revitalizes Luhmann's systems theory approach to intimate relationships and love as communication media in modern societies. It invites scholars to apply systems-theoretical concepts to examine contemporary transformations of intimate life across different sociocultural contexts, bridging gaps between geographically or culturally isolated scholarly conversations.

Contributions may adopt two perspectives: analyzing intimate systems through systems theory concepts and examining how other social systems (law, politics, media, education) observe and shape intimacies. The special issue welcomes diverse empirical work grounded in theoretical frameworks, particularly from varied sociocultural environments.

metaTitle: Observing the Future: Systems Theory Meets Science Fiction
title: Observing the Future: Systems Theory Meets Science Fiction
topics: Investigations into the 'hypertrophy' of social subsystems (e.g., totalitarization of politics, economization of life) and dedifferentiation in utopian and dystopian literature
The emergence of non-human communicative systems, including Artificial Intelligence and alien consciousness, and their structural coupling with human society
Science fiction as a specific function of the art system, allowing society to observe its own evolution, paradoxes, and latent possibilities
Systems-theoretic readings of ecological crisis, the environment, and global interdependencies in speculative fiction
Examining the fragmentation of public discourse, 'echo chambers,' and the breakdown of communication through the lens of SF narratives

paragraphs: This special issue bridges systems theory and science fiction criticism to analyze speculative narratives as models of complex social systems. The editors argue that while science fiction commonly receives sociological interpretation, systematic application of Niklas Luhmann's theory and second-order cybernetics to the genre remains underexplored. The collection seeks to demonstrate how science fiction uniquely simulates social dynamics, including autopoiesis, operational closure, and functional differentiation, addressing contemporary concerns around artificial intelligence, fragmented discourse, and interconnected systems.

The issue invites interdisciplinary scholarship examining how science fiction depicts functional differentiation across social subsystems and explores scenarios where particular subsystems become hyperextended. Contributors should investigate the modeling of non-human communicative systems and their relationship to human society, as well as treat science fiction as the art system's mechanism for observing social evolution and latent possibilities. The collection welcomes diverse approaches that test systems theory's explanatory capacity through engagement with imaginative science fiction narratives.

journal: International Journal of Managing Projects in Business
metaTitle: People at the Heart of Projectification: Rethinking Agency, Identity, and Value Creation​
title: People at the Heart of Projectification: Rethinking Agency, Identity, and Value Creation
topics: How do individuals implement and negotiate their agency in the context of increasing projectification by navigating between structure, temporality, and autonomy?
How do individuals build and maintain their identities amid the fluidity and temporality of projectified work in a complex social environment?
How do people co-create and redefine value through their participation in - and contribution to - the ongoing projectification in our society?
What role do projects play in the development of people, from childhood to old age? Is there any difference between personal and occupational development?
How do different levels of education and educational opportunities affect people's participation in projects and projectification?
What expectations, aspirations, and objectives do individuals pursue through their involvement in projects, project management, and projectification?
What impact (positive and/or negative) does engagement in projects - as temporary endeavors - have on the people involved?
Which prerequisites have to be created by organizations, government, or society so that people engage in projects and turn them into success stories?
How much projectification can people tolerate, or is there a point at which over-projectification is reached and de-projectification starts?
How do cultural factors affect people's involvement in projects and projectification?
What are the main differences in projectification across the globe, and how does it influence individuals involved or eager to enter the project world?
To what extent is the use of professional project management beneficial or detrimental to the implementation of projects in the different areas of society?

paragraphs: Projectification—the embedding of project logic across organizations, public sectors, and society—has fundamentally transformed how work is organized. While this shift has been widely documented, scholarly attention has predominantly focused on systemic and organizational dimensions, often overlooking the human experience. This special issue seeks to redress this imbalance by centering individuals and their experiences within projectification processes.

The issue invites interdisciplinary contributions exploring how people exercise agency, construct identity, and create value within projectified contexts. It addresses researchers and practitioners interested in understanding the lived experiences of those who shape, participate in, or are affected by projectification across educational, occupational, cultural, and geographical contexts.

journal: International Journal of Public Sector Management

paragraphs: Administrative burdens—the learning, compliance, and psychological costs citizens face when interacting with government—have become a significant research area. These burdens disproportionately affect vulnerable groups and threaten administrative equity, particularly in welfare systems. Scholars are increasingly investigating strategies to reduce or mitigate these burdens, including fostering citizen resources through intermediaries and improving organizational design and communication practices.

This special issue seeks contributions examining burden-reduction initiatives undertaken by various actors across different contexts and levels of governance. It welcomes research investigating how public organizations, managers, and street-level bureaucrats can reduce administrative burdens, which interventions are effective, whether they benefit all groups equally, and how burden-reduction efforts are perceived within public administration. The issue aims to generate societal impact by addressing challenges relevant to practitioners and policymakers working to reduce administrative burdens.

journal: Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
metaTitle: Reimaging Entrepreneurship Education in the Era of Disruptive Emerging Technologies

Institutional Integration and Capacity Building - Organizational capabilities enabling technology adoption; leadership and faculty preparedness; university-industry collaboration models; digital infrastructure development; government policies and regulatory frameworks; creating entrepreneurial ecosystems beyond traditional classrooms

Curriculum Design and Assessment Innovation - Assessment methods for technology-integrated learning environments; addressing generative AI in student evaluation; metrics for measuring impact on learning outcomes and business creation; longitudinal studies on career development; cost-effectiveness evaluation; educator training and professional development models

paragraphs: Entrepreneurship education must adapt to rapid technological change, as emerging innovations like AI, blockchain, and immersive platforms are fundamentally transforming how entrepreneurs identify opportunities, develop prototypes, and scale businesses. While these technologies offer unprecedented pedagogical potential through simulations and gamified learning, many educational programs continue using traditional, Western-centric approaches that prioritize information delivery over experiential learning.

This special issue addresses the urgent need to critically examine how entrepreneurship education can effectively integrate emerging technologies while remaining responsive to the entrepreneurial realities students will face. The issue is particularly relevant for emerging economies, where digital tools can overcome infrastructure limitations and resource constraints to democratize access to quality entrepreneurship education, though success requires institutional capacity building, thoughtful curriculum design, and supporting policies.

metaTitle: Research with Impact: Qualitative approaches to social and behaviour change
title: Research with Impact: Qualitative approaches to social and behaviour change

Develop longitudinal qualitative frameworks to demonstrate the social impact of ethical interventions and inclusive social marketing strategies

paragraphs: This special issue seeks to demonstrate how qualitative and interpretive research can drive meaningful social and behavioural change, particularly for underrepresented and marginalised groups. Rather than relying solely on quantitative metrics, the collection aims to show how deep qualitative inquiry uncovers the psychological and cultural factors that shape human behaviour and can inform ethical, inclusive interventions that address complex social problems.

The call reflects growing recognition that qualitative research must evolve to engage participatory and inclusive frameworks, especially when working with neurodivergent, trauma-affected, and marginalised populations. The special issue responds to an urgent need for research methodologies that empower rather than merely study neglected communities, drawing on approaches such as netnography and community-led participatory methods to create transformative social impact.

journal: Journal of Small Business and Enterprise Development

paragraphs: Digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and sustainability pressures are reshaping how entrepreneurs access capital and how value is created and financed. These changes have created new financing mechanisms while raising questions about equity and access to funding for small businesses and startups, particularly regarding collateral, legitimacy, and institutional visibility.

The special issue addresses emerging financing channels such as crowdfunding, peer-to-peer lending, and tokenized assets, while emphasizing that financial decisions are influenced by behavioral, social, institutional, and sustainability factors beyond technical considerations. Artificial intelligence is a key focus, as it transforms credit evaluation, investment screening, and venture creation, affecting SMEs' access to finance and requiring interdisciplinary approaches.

The special issue seeks multidisciplinary research deepening understanding of how digitalization, AI, and sustainability pressures reshape entrepreneurial finance. It welcomes conceptual articles, literature reviews, and empirical studies using various methods, targeting scholars and practitioners including entrepreneurs, SME managers, investors, policymakers, and financial intermediaries.

journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting & Financial Management

paragraphs: Local governments play a crucial role in public service delivery and resource management, yet their financial management and accountability have traditionally been studied within national frameworks. Recent cross-national initiatives have made internationally comparable data more accessible, though existing analyses primarily focus on macroeconomic perspectives rather than managerial and operational dimensions at the individual local government level. This special issue seeks to advance understanding of how local governments manage finances and ensure accountability across different national and institutional contexts.

The field of comparative local government finance research remains underdeveloped, constrained by diverse legal, administrative, and political systems across countries. A comparative approach enables examination of how institutional settings, fiscal arrangements, and governance traditions shape financial management practices, facilitates identification of best practices that can be adapted to different contexts, and builds theories applicable across national borders. The special issue invites conceptual, empirical, and policy-oriented contributions that address barriers to comparability and explore practical solutions for strengthening local financial governance globally.

paragraphs: Organizations face unprecedented challenges from uncertainty, technological change, and shifting work arrangements. This special issue calls for researchers to revisit fundamental HRM theories and examine whether established assumptions adequately explain the relationship between people, organizations, and performance in today's turbulent context. The issue seeks to move beyond incremental complexity by returning to core concepts and critically assessing whether traditional perspectives on HRM-strategy alignment, employee development, and performance outcomes remain sufficient.

The special issue welcomes theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous contributions that challenge conventional HRM wisdom and propose new understandings relevant to uncertain environments. Research may address tensions and unintended consequences of HRM practices, sustainability concerns, digitalization, employee well-being, and emerging employment models. Empirical studies, conceptual papers, and literature reviews are all welcome, provided they offer clear advances to HRM theory and research.

metaTitle: Sustainable Paths in Digital Supply Chains: Navigating Environmental Challenges and Technological Frontiers

paragraphs: This special issue examines how digital technologies can be integrated with sustainability objectives in modern supply chains. Organizations are increasingly pressured to reduce environmental impacts and ensure ethical operations while managing technological disruption. The issue explores how emerging tools like artificial intelligence, blockchain, and data analytics can enhance supply chain transparency, efficiency, emissions monitoring, and resilience while addressing climate risks and regulatory demands.

The collection seeks empirical, conceptual, and methodological contributions that bridge theory and practice in digital sustainability transitions. It recognizes that technological adoption alone is insufficient; successful transformation requires supportive leadership, training, and organizational culture change. The special issue draws on multiple theoretical perspectives to provide comprehensive understanding of how human and organizational factors influence sustainability-driven digitalization across different organizational contexts.

The issue addresses pressing challenges including climate change mitigation, responsible production, and ethical governance, aligning with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. It invites interdisciplinary dialogue among scholars, practitioners, and policymakers to advance both academic knowledge and practical solutions for organizations navigating environmental challenges through digital innovation.

paragraphs: Organizations face increasing complexity from shifting geopolitical, economic, and technological conditions, requiring strategic approaches to knowledge management for sustainability. The integration of knowledge management with AI offers potential benefits for problem-solving and decision-making, yet presents challenges that require responsible and ethical implementation. This special issue examines how organizations can leverage strategic knowledge management to balance the opportunities and risks of AI while maintaining sustainability across their operations.

The call seeks contributions exploring how organizations can effectively manage both human knowledge and AI-generated intelligent knowledge, addressing issues such as knowledge overload, loss, and duplication. It emphasizes the importance of codification and personalization strategies that align with organizational values and objectives. The special issue invites researchers to examine how sustainable strategic knowledge management enables organizations to adapt to rapidly changing environments while achieving economic, social, and environmental goals.

metaTitle: The Architecture of Meaning: Reconstructing Luhmann’s Dimensional Framework
title: The Architecture of Meaning: Reconstructing Luhmann's Dimensional Framework
topics: Theoretical work revisiting or extending established three-dimensional models of meaning (factual, temporal, social), including introduction of novel distinctions such as spatial, modal, or motivational dimensions and expanded sub-programmes within systems theory
Studies focusing on second-order observation, reflexivity, and the inherent paradoxes of observation within social and psychic systems
Analyses of how artificial intelligence, artificial communication, and algorithmic decision premises impact meaning-processing systems, technological co-evolution, and structures of expectation
Explorations of forms of meaning that resist operational closure, reduction, or authoritarian simplification, including the role of imagination, counterfactuals, and non-necessary social orders

Systems-theoretical approaches to current societal challenges, encompassing values, political polarisation, populism, inter-systemic relations, strategies for complexity reduction, and pathologies of meaninglessness

Renewed theoretical and empirical engagement with sense-making, consciousness, psychology, and psychotherapy, with a focus on identity formation and the structural coupling between psychic and social systems

paragraphs: This special issue examines Luhmann's concept of meaning as a central medium for both psychic and social systems, structured across three canonical dimensions: factual, temporal, and social. The call argues that while these three dimensions are foundational to systems theory, the underlying logic of why meaning should be organized into exactly these three dimensions remains unresolved. Recent scholarship suggests that meaning may be better understood as a potentially expandable framework responding to basic questions of observation, with additional dimensions such as spatial, modal, and motivational warranting exploration.

The special issue aims to revisit and extend meaning theory in response to contemporary societal complexities, particularly the technological mediation of meaning through artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems, as well as challenges like polarization and meaninglessness. It invites interdisciplinary contributions that employ reflexivity and second-order observation to explore how meaning is currently being observed, transformed, and contested across different media and inter-systemic relations.

journal: Journal of Enterprising Communities: People and Places in the Global Economy

paragraphs: This special issue examines how emotions influence entrepreneurial judgment and decision-making, particularly in community-based and localized ecosystems. While existing research has focused on positive emotions like passion and resilience, the issue seeks to explore understudied emotional domains such as despair, awe, humility, guilt, empathy, and regret that shape entrepreneurs' strategic choices, resilience, and ethical judgments.

The special issue welcomes interdisciplinary research on how diverse emotional experiences affect entrepreneurial cognition and behavior within small businesses, family firms, and social enterprises. It invites both quantitative approaches examining causal relationships and qualitative studies exploring contextualized experiences, alongside theoretical contributions offering new frameworks for understanding emotions in entrepreneurship.

Insights from this research aim to inform policy-making, entrepreneurial education, and support structures by revealing how emotional dynamics drive sustainable business practices, ethical decision-making, and community engagement in localized entrepreneurial ecosystems.

journal: VINE Journal of Information and Knowledge Management Systems
metaTitle: The role of social capital in knowledge management

paragraphs: This special issue explores the interconnection between social capital and knowledge management in organizations. Social capital—networks of relationships, trust, and shared norms—facilitates knowledge exchange and integration, enhancing intellectual capital development and organizational competitiveness across sectors including technology, finance, healthcare, and creative industries.

The call addresses critical research gaps including the lack of general theory explaining how social capital translates to intellectual capital across different contexts, inconsistent measurement approaches, and limited longitudinal studies. It seeks contributions examining how social capital functions as a mediating mechanism in digital environments, how it evolves over time, and how cultural and technological factors influence these dynamics.

The special issue invites empirical and theoretical research from academics and practitioners investigating social capital's role in knowledge creation, innovation outcomes, and competitive advantage, with particular attention to measurement frameworks, trust mechanisms, and organizational structures that enable effective knowledge management.

metaTitle: The Systemic Paradox of Democracy: Cybernetics, Threat and Resilience in Complex Governance
title: The Systemic Paradox of Democracy: Cybernetics, Threat and Resilience in Complex Governance
topics: Democracy as a self-referential and paradoxical system
Democratic resilience, backsliding, institutional learning and adaptation

Disinformation, AI, digital platforms and democratic communication

Normative and design implications for reflexive, resilient and trustworthy democratic governance

paragraphs: This special issue examines democracy through a systems-theoretical lens, addressing the structural tension between democratic openness and the need to manage threats to institutions and public order. The editors invite contributions that apply cybernetics and complexity theory to understand how democratic systems observe, communicate about and respond to various pressures including war, pandemics, disinformation, migration and technological disruption.

The issue seeks to integrate perspectives from multiple fields including democratic theory, governance, securitisation studies, media research and resilience thinking. It particularly welcomes work that moves beyond linear explanations to analyse feedback loops, recursive processes and unintended consequences of governance interventions, examining paradoxes such as liberty versus security and inclusion versus exclusion.

A key focus is developing systems-theoretical vocabulary for understanding democratic resilience as something more than mere recovery—work that explores how democratic systems learn, reinterpret threat, maintain legitimacy and reorganise decision-making while preserving pluralism. The issue is designed for conceptual papers, empirical studies and methodological contributions.

metaTitle: Beyond the Island: The Rise of Project Ecosystems
title: Beyond the Island: The Rise of Project Ecosystems
