metaTitle: Management Learning invites submissions for Special Issue Immanent Critique in Management Learning and Education
title: Immanent Critique in Management Learning and Education: Organizational Contradictions, Emancipatory Possibilities, and Institutional Transformation
topics: Theoretical contributions developing immanent critique for MLE contexts
Scholarship examining how management education's contradictions relate to broader transformations in capitalism, knowledge production, and subjectivity formation
Efforts to rework immanent critique through decolonial, indigenous, and/or feminist epistemologies to address its Western/male-dominated philosophical origins
Efforts to develop conceptual frameworks for understanding emancipatory learning within constrained institutional contexts
Analyses of how business school commitments to sustainability, EDI, or social responsibility play out in curricular design, pedagogical practice, and institutional governance

Studies of alternative institutional forms of management learning, such as cooperatives, free universities, worker-owned schools, platform-cooperative training programs, indigenous-led and faith-based business education

Critical investigations of the effects of the rise of far-right political leaders on progressive initiatives in education, such as EDI initiatives, equal pay and promotions, sustainability and ESG measures, and campus protests

Studies of the pedagogy of growth taught alongside curricula on planetary boundaries, ecological economics, and post-growth alternatives
Analyses of sustainability and ESG modules as moments of managerial absorption rather than ecological reckoning
Engagements with climate-justice movements as sources of immanent normative reconstruction inside the business school

paragraphs: This special issue addresses an underexplored concern in Management Learning and Education (MLE): the contradictions between the emancipatory ideals espoused by business schools and the institutional, ideological and economic logics they reproduce. Critics have charged MLE with neoliberal, colonial, racist, and sexist practices, which reproduce the harms and injustices of capitalism. However important such work is, these critiques have largely been mounted from a position external to the institutions they target. Less examined is how transformation may be pursued from inside MLE itself, by holding business schools accountable to the very ideals they profess.

The tension is fundamental. Business schools operate as market-driven enterprises while proclaiming educational missions centred on ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility. They continue to train the architects and lackeys of an economic system breaching planetary boundaries while housing sustainability modules that rarely examine the growth imperative running through the wider curriculum. But even though the gap between ecological pedagogy and the ecological consequences of business-as-usual education has become a defining contradiction of the field, such instability also opens space for reimagining the purpose and practice of management education. Institutions that fail to do so risk obsolescence, with their academic freedom further eroded by political intervention or being outdone by AI tools that beat them at their own game of dubious knowledge creation.

Immanent critique offers a particularly valuable method to work through these contradictions and the transformational possibilities that they harbour. In essence, immanent critique combines internal critique with normative critique. Whereas internal critique involves thorough empirical analysis to identify dissonance between institutional claims and reality, normative critique appeals to standards reconstructed from, or held up against, the institution itself. This dual approach lets scholars identify discrepancies between stated missions and operational realities while judging institutions against broader standards of justice and sustainability. Unlike external critique, which imposes outside standards, or ideology critique, which assumes that participants are deluded by false consciousness, immanent critique examines institutions from the inside.

Two things complicate the exercise of immanent critique in business schools. Firstly, business schools speak polyvocally through voices that often pull in opposing directions (through accreditation regimes, faculty research cultures, student demands, donor expectations, etc.). As a result, immanent critique in MLE is no neutral mirroring of declared values but requires careful reconstruction of institutional normativity. Secondly, immanent critique involves the everyday practices of faculty, students, and staff without being confined to the classroom. Such praxis may be enacted on the margins of business schools, through climate occupations and divestment campaigns, anti-war encampments, decolonial reading groups, sanctuary classrooms, strike action and curricular sabotage. Used this way, immanent critique offers a way of revitalising MLE not by indicting it from outside but by internal engagement for institutional transformation.

Working through the internal and external contradictions of business schools, immanent critique turns tensions into pedagogical resources. When business schools claim to educate ethical leaders while prioritising profit maximisation, students can examine organisational hypocrisy not simply as the moral failure of individuals but as structural contradictions requiring systemic solutions. Historical precedent supports this approach: business schools themselves were born of contradictions between professional training and academic legitimacy; contradictions between theory and practice gave way to innovations such as the case method and interdisciplinary curricula. Although these transformations were neither uncontested nor unequivocally emancipatory, they do point to the capacity of MLE to be reconstituted through, rather than against, its internal tensions. Today's challenges call for a similarly fundamental reimagining of purpose and pedagogy.

Methodologically, immanent critique can be pursued through a plurality of approaches. Ethnography is well suited to surfacing contradictions between what people say and what they do, but historical and archival analysis, textual and discursive reconstruction, participatory action research, philosophical reconstruction of institutional norms, and arts-based inquiry are equally legitimate paths into the same problem. By centring the experiences of those inside MLE, immanent critique builds theory from practice and helps close the theory-practice divide in critical management research. The empirical exposition of institutional contradictions also facilitates critique-in-use, that is, forms of critical practice that enable emancipatory change by collectively creating the conditions in which new thinking and new forms of organising may emerge.

metaTitle: Modern Family Firms
title: Modern Family Firms: The Missing Piece in Family Business Studies
topics: Reconceptualizing Modern Family Firms' Processes and Outcomes - Understanding how a 'modern family firm' is defined and how it makes entrepreneurial and strategic decisions
How is the concept of 'modern family' defined in family business literature? To what extent does family business literature consider the modern family structure as a variable of interest?
Are modern family structures more or less prone than traditional ones to entrepreneurial and strategic actions?
How do economic and noneconomic-related goals evolve in relation to the evolution of the modern family structure?
Are modern family structures more prone than traditional ones to long-term orientation and continuity or exit?

Modern Family Firms and Transgenerational Entrepreneurship and Succession - How do alternative incumbent-successor relationships impact transgenerational entrepreneurship and succession in modern family firms?
How do modern parental behaviors affect transgenerational entrepreneurship and succession?
How do succession strategies differ within modern family firms compared to traditional family firms?
Is each successor in a modern family firm treated equally?

Modern Family Firms and Institutional Constraints - Which existing theories and perspectives can illuminate modern family dynamics and outcomes in the context of each country's institutional constraints?
How do institutional constraints affect relationships among family members in modern business families?
How do succession arrangements differ between modern and traditional business families across various countries?
How do institutional constraints within a country affect the migration and emergence of modern business families in other countries?

paragraphs: Ninety-nine percent of family business articles tend to justify their studies by stating that the majority of businesses in the world are family firms and often assume that family is defined as a nuclear or extended traditional family bound by socio-legal obligations. However, sociologists have extensively explained how various changes—cultural, economic, social, political, and demographic—have influenced the formation, arrangement, and meaning of different family configurations. Research and government reports have primarily documented the phenomenon of decreasing marriages and increasing divorces, as well as the impact of new alternative living arrangements on public opinions and social behaviors. This includes same-sex marriages, single-parent families, different/same-sex common-law couples, and post-divorce and blended families. Family science scholars have also highlighted the rise and prevalence of stepfamilies compared to first-marriage families.

Despite these significant shifts in family structures, extant family business literature seems to not care. When examining family firm behaviors, social relationships, structures, and processes such as succession, scholars tend to assume and search for a traditional family structure beyond the business. They typically exclude the possibility that alternative living arrangements might affect family firm dynamics and processes. With few emerging exceptions, the question of how modern family arrangements affect family organizational dynamics, business strategies, and outcomes remains largely ignored in the literature.

This special issue on Modern Family Firms aims to open a critical and contemporary debate on modern family firms—specifically, those owned and managed by modern families. This initiative challenges the numerous in-house assumptions and current perspectives that overlook the evolving nature of traditional families into modern family structures. The special issue will provoke and advance family business and entrepreneurship research, encouraging scholars to consider alternative family arrangements and their effects on decision-makers' behaviors and firm outcomes.

The topic aligns well with the journal's scope, as it holds significant potential to enhance family business research given the substantial transformation of family firms from traditional to modern, reflecting the evolution of the family unit from the classic nuclear model to more contemporary forms. This special issue invites papers that can deepen understanding of the changing nature of the family concept and its consequences for family firms. The investigation aims to uncover the nuances of modern family dynamics and their influence on family business strategies, decision-making processes, and overall firm outcomes, including structures and procedures designed to manage family involvement, succession planning, gender equality, and the preservation of family unity alongside pursuing economic objectives.

Rigorous theorizing and incorporating insights from disciplines such as sociology, psychology, neuroscience, history, anthropology, and family science is key to succeed in this endeavor. Both theoretical and empirical works using various methodological approaches are welcomed, including qualitative methods, phenomenography, ethnography, policy capturing, experiments and replications, and quantitative analyses.

metaTitle: Multinational Enterprises and the Sustainable Development Goals
title: Multinational Enterprises and the Sustainable Development Goals: Evolving Roles, Challenges, and Opportunities Beyond 2030
topics: MNEs' Evolving Role in the SDGs' Agenda: Achievements, Gaps, and Future Directions - How can MNEs evaluate their contributions to the SDGs and adjust their strategies to meet the 2030 targets? What opportunities and challenges will MNEs face post-2030 in continuing to support the SDGs' agenda? How can MNEs address the lagging targets of the SDGs in their operations?

Managing ESG Backlash and its impact on MNEs' SDGs' Alignment - How does the ESG backlash impact MNEs' strategies for achieving the SDGs? In what ways do political and institutional pressures shape MNEs' SDG agendas? How can MNEs maintain their commitment to the SDGs amidst the growing scepticism toward ESG?

Institutional Dynamics and MNEs' SDGs' Engagement - How do formal and informal institutional logics influence MNEs' strategies for addressing SDGs in different host countries? How do institutional voids in emerging markets shape MNEs' SDG engagement? What roles do institutional actors (governments, NGOs, civil society) play in shaping MNEs' SDG commitments?

Business and Society Perspectives on MNEs and SDGs: Bridging IB and B&S Literature - How can IB literature inform B&S's understandings of MNEs' contributions to SDGs? How do MNEs reconcile profit motives with societal goals in their SDGs' strategies? What are the synergies between business model innovation and sustainable development in the context of the SDGs?

Leveraging Global Value Chains for Sustainable Development - What practical strategies can MNEs adopt to integrate sustainability into their global value chains to meet SDGs' targets? What are the opportunities for MNEs to collaborate with supply chain partners on SDGs' initiatives? How can knowledge transfer across value chains improve SDGs' outcomes?

Organizational Forms and Alliance for SDGs: Bridging IB and BAS Perspectives - How can MNEs and their partners in cross-sector alliances navigate the challenges of aligning values, beliefs, and power dynamics in SDG-driven initiatives? In what ways can partnerships between MNEs, governments, NGOs, and CSOs enhance the achievement of SDGs, particularly in areas such as inclusive development and climate action? What role do MNE headquarters play in supporting subsidiaries and local network partners to integrate global sustainability principles into their operations? How can MNEs collaborate with SMEs to achieve SDGs, and what benefits does this collaboration bring to local communities? How do strategic alliances contribute to the long-term sustainability of SDG initiatives, and what organizational forms are most effective in fostering these collaborations?

Micro-foundations of MNEs' Engagement with SDGs: Motivations, Leadership, and Human Capital - How do the personal experiences and values of top management, including the CEO, influence MNEs' strategies for addressing the SDGs? What role does diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) play in shaping top management's engagement with sustainability goals and advancing SDGs? How do leadership styles and top management teams influence employee engagement with SDG initiatives within MNEs? What mechanisms within MNEs' governance structures support or hinder the integration of SDGs into business models, particularly in the areas of poverty eradication, climate action, and social equity? How do individual decision-makers contribute to business model innovations that advance SDGs, and how do these innovations affect the company's long-term sustainability efforts?

paragraphs: The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, provide a comprehensive global agenda addressing critical social, economic, and environmental challenges, with the target of achieving these goals by 2030. These 17 interconnected goals range from eradicating poverty and ensuring quality education to combating climate change and fostering sustainable economic growth. As the global community works toward this ambitious target, the role of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs) has become increasingly vital. MNEs, with their significant financial resources, innovation capabilities, and extensive global reach, are uniquely positioned to contribute meaningfully to the realization of these global objectives. However, integrating the SDGs into business strategies presents considerable challenges, especially in light of evolving institutional, political, and social dynamics.

In this context, it is essential to critically assess the progress made by MNEs in supporting the SDGs, focusing not only on successes but also on areas where progress has stalled or where the current trajectory requires recalibration. As the world struggles to meet the deadline for the SDG agenda, there is an urgent need to reassess the contributions of MNEs and to explore how these enterprises can adapt in response to the shifting global landscape. This will ensure that MNEs' operations remain aligned with the sustainability and social equity goals. Additionally, the rise of backlash against Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) initiatives presents new challenges that may influence MNEs' strategies, especially their long-term commitment to the SDGs as we move beyond 2030.

This special issue aims to explore the evolving and multifaceted role of MNEs in advancing the SDGs, with a dual focus on the remaining years of the current SDG agenda and the post-2030 sustainability framework. We aim to assess how MNEs can contribute meaningfully to achieving the SDGs by 2030 while addressing the complexities of changing political, social, and economic contexts. Furthermore, how these enterprises will adapt to, and engage in shaping, sustainability frameworks beyond 2030, particularly given the shifting global trends and the growing scepticism surrounding ESG commitments.

MNEs are critical enablers of global sustainability due to their market power, innovation potential, and financial resources. With their global value chains spanning several nations, MNEs influence the markets in which they operate and impact the communities. As key players in industrial transformation, they can drive positive change by aligning their business strategies with the SDGs. Their ability to innovate, scale sustainable practices, and set industry standards enables them to be significant actors in addressing global challenges, such as climate change, poverty, and inequality. They can drive disruptive societal change through their global experience.

However, MNEs' involvement in the SDGs must extend beyond mere profit-driven motives. To contribute effectively to the SDGs, MNEs must prioritize inclusive business practices and environmental stewardship, ensuring that their operations create shared value across economic, social, and environmental dimensions. This involves addressing global inequalities through inclusive business models, promoting responsible production and consumption, and investing in sustainable innovations that mitigate long-term global risks, such as resource depletion, biodiversity loss, and climate change.

Integrating the SDGs into business operations is a complex and multifaceted endeavour. MNEs face several barriers, including institutional inertia, political uncertainties, and varying regulatory frameworks across different markets. The political economy of each host country significantly influences how effectively SDGs can be pursued, particularly in regions with weak governance systems or where sustainability initiatives are not adequately incentivized. Moreover, cross-sector collaboration models that are often considered essential for addressing complex SDG challenges can be hindered by competing interests or regulatory barriers.

Internally, MNEs face challenges aligning sustainability strategies with shareholder interests. The increasing pressure to deliver short-term financial performance can sometimes conflict with the long-term investments required for sustainable development. Measuring the impact of MNE activities on the SDGs also presents a significant challenge, with accountability and transparency emerging as critical issues. While frameworks for impact measurement and reporting are still evolving, many MNEs struggle to quantify their contributions to the SDGs in ways that are meaningful to stakeholders.

As we approach the final years of the SDG agenda, it is important to critically reflect on the lessons learned thus far and evaluate where gaps remain. While many MNEs have made significant strides toward integrating the SDGs into their operations, the pace of change has been uneven across industries and regions. For instance, in sectors such as renewable energy, MNEs have made substantial contributions toward achieving SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy). In contrast, other areas, such as climate action (SDG 13) and responsible consumption (SDG 12), still face significant challenges.

Looking beyond 2030, the post-SDG sustainability framework will necessitate that MNEs adapt to an increasingly complex landscape. Political shifts, economic transformations, and societal changes are likely to continue shaping the global sustainability agenda. Evolving ESG expectations, alongside the increasing backlash against these initiatives, will play a pivotal role in shaping how businesses engage with the SDGs. As societal expectations around climate action, diversity, and corporate responsibility grow, MNEs will need to navigate a delicate balance between business imperatives and public expectations.

This dynamic context requires MNEs to adopt a long-term perspective, committing to sustainable business practices that focus not only on short-term financial returns but also on their broader impact on global sustainability. The post-2030 agenda may require MNEs to take on more active roles in developing global frameworks for climate action, economic inclusivity, and social equity, with greater accountability and transparency in reporting their contributions toward these goals.

The evolving role of MNEs in shaping global sustainability frameworks necessitates an integrated approach to International Business (IB) and Business and Society (BAS) scholarship. By merging insights from the IB and societal domains, a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that drive MNEs' engagement with the SDGs can be developed, alongside the mechanisms through which they can exert influence. Understanding the interplay between these factors is crucial for both academia and practitioners, who seek to guide MNEs toward more effective sustainability practices that drive tangible, long-term impacts.

By examining both the successes and shortcomings of MNEs in relation to the SDGs, this special issue aims to explore strategies for scaling successful initiatives, overcoming barriers, and adapting to a rapidly changing global environment. The goal is to provide actionable insights that can guide MNEs in navigating the complex terrain of SDGs' integration and contribute to the development of a post-2030 sustainability framework that is inclusive, equitable, and resilient in the face of future challenges.

metaTitle: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
title: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
topics: How Organizations Integrate the Planetary Boundary Framework into Strategy and Action

How theory on circular and regenerative systems can be informed by considering planetary boundaries

paragraphs: Scholarship on business sustainability increasingly views organizations as embedded within natural systems, conceptualized through the planetary boundaries framework. The planetary boundary framework defines nine Earth system processes that regulate the planet's stability and resilience and are directly affected by human activity. Alarmingly, seven of these nine boundaries have now been crossed, threatening both natural systems and the economies that depend on them. For business scholarship, this creates an urgent need to understand how organizations can operate and manage within the safe space delineated by planetary boundaries.

Much prior research on the natural environment in management has privileged firm-level outcomes such as financial performance and has overlooked the complex, coupled dynamics of ecological, social, and organizational systems. Drawing from ecology and biophysical system science, the planetary boundary framework provides both the conceptual and empirical depth to address this complexity and a scientifically grounded map of global limits to study how organizations affect — and are affected by — key ecological processes. It also serves as a boundary tool that enables interdisciplinary collaboration between management scholars and natural scientists.

Business scholars and practitioners increasingly recognize the need for deeper insight into sustainability that treats natural systems as operational and strategic constraints, as seen in rising attention to practical efforts such as the Science Based Targets Initiative to help companies align with planetary boundaries. However, integrating the planetary boundary framework into organizational research remains a challenge. One reason is that management research has largely been grounded in organization-focused theories and social science methodologies, with limited engagement with the natural sciences as a conceptual or empirical foundation. As a result, despite a growing body of work, a cohesive understanding of how the planetary boundary framework can bring the biophysical to the fore in organizational scholarship is still lacking.

This Special Issue responds to this gap by advancing the integration of the planetary boundary framework into management research and accelerating actionable insights into how organizations, their leaders, and the communities they affect can operate within planetary boundaries. The central question is: How can the planetary boundary framework be leveraged to develop theory and practice that illuminate the embeddedness of organizations within natural systems? Contributions should move beyond treating the natural environment as mere context, to position planetary boundaries as core organizing principles for theorizing, measuring, and guiding organizational action.

The Special Issue aims to spark scholarship that develops new concepts and empirical evidence grounded in biophysical system science; examines how organizations, industries, governments, and communities contribute to, or help avert, planetary boundary transgressions; and explores governance and innovation pathways that enable organizations to thrive while remaining within a safe and just operating space. The special issue sets out to push other boundaries too: the combined interdisciplinary networks of the guest editors allow drawing on natural scientists as readers, contributors, and reviewers to ensure reliable scientific evidence.

Both theoretical and empirical submissions from across business sustainability research are invited, with particular interest in studies that examine how organizations engage with biophysical limits and operate within the safe space defined by the planetary boundaries framework, leveraging planetary boundary concepts, models, or data to inform strategy, decision-making, and policy engagement. Studies investigating how organizations develop proactive and responsive strategies to address the interconnections between planetary boundaries and social issues, and studies that synthesize empirical insights from organizations and engage in forward-looking theorizing about how the planetary boundary framework could reshape organizing are welcome.

Research that emerges from collaboration with natural scientists or applies natural science methods and measures such as geospatial data, biodiversity and genetic diversity indicators is especially encouraged. While management research has focused heavily on climate change, papers addressing the other eight planetary boundaries are particularly welcome, including biosphere integrity, freshwater change, land-system change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading, and novel entities.

metaTitle: Our Oceans as a Business-Society Nexus
title: Our Oceans as a Business-Society Nexus: Advancing the Interplay of Blue Economy, Blue Governance and Blue Justice
topics: Business models, value creation, and distribution: How do different ocean-based business models create value, who captures the value and who bears costs across communities, ecosystems, and value/supply chains? What trade-offs and paradoxes emerge between economic growth and social/environmental objectives, and how are they justified, negotiated, or contested by various stakeholders and at different levels? How do firms build, maintain, or lose social licence to operate in ocean- and coast-related activities, and what triggers shifts in legitimacy?

Governance, accountability, and power across levels: How do governance arrangements (e.g., local, national, regional, transnational) shape who gets access, who is included/excluded, and how rules are enforced in ocean and coastal settings? When and why do 'good governance' arrangements still produce undesired social outcomes (e.g., exclusion, livelihood disruption), and what mechanisms explain this? How do firms, states, NGOs, and community actors coordinate or compete to frame problems, set standards, and allocate responsibilities and resources?

Justice, equity, and lived impacts: How are distributive, procedural, recognitional, and restorative justice concerns expressed in ocean and coastal contexts, and how do they translate into organisational and policy decisions? What forms of inequity arise in practice (e.g., displacement, access restrictions, benefit-sharing), and what interventions have been effective (or ineffective) in redressing them? How do gender, indigeneity, and marginalisation shape participation in governance and benefit-sharing, and what organisational and policy practices enable or constrain inclusion?

Ownership, stewardship, and legitimacy: Under what conditions are oceans treated as shared spaces versus commodified resources, and how do firms and states influence these framings? What governance designs or institutional arrangements support credible stewardship (beyond compliance), and how are these maintained or evolve over time? How do alternative understandings of stewardship and collective rights (including Indigenous governance) reshape corporate strategy, accountability, and legitimacy?

Risk, contestation, and the 'dark side': How do illegal, informal, or harmful practices (e.g., illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, labour abuses, illicit trade) become embedded in ocean-related industries, and what enables accountability or impunity? How do firms manage reputational, legal, and operational risks linked to ocean-related activities, and when do risk-management approaches conflict with justice and sustainability aims?

paragraphs: Our oceans make up 70% of our planet, provide transportation for 80% of global goods in volume and ensure the livelihood of over 3 billion people, including many of the global poor. Oceans represent the largest environment-humanity nexus on Earth in environmental, economic, geopolitical and global security, and socio-cultural terms. Yet, as planetary spaces, our oceans are often thought of as separate from humans in a human-nature duality, which limits research on the place-space embeddedness of business in particular environmental materialities like our oceans.

Despite the critical role played by the world's oceans, management scholarship has engaged with oceanic contexts in a relatively limited and uneven way. Existing contributions have frequently framed ocean-based activities through blue growth lenses centred on economic value and growth under the banner of neo-classical capitalism, which promotes the exploitation of common pool resources, erodes public goods and incentivizes business to externalize costs. Given that over 60% of our oceans are considered international waters beyond national jurisdictions, these dynamics are especially salient in oceanic contexts, which helps to explain their depletion and the prevalence of various kinds of socio-economic injustices.

Despite their critical role for the Planet, our oceans are economically exploited by a small number of powerful state and business actors. For example, over 80% of global fishing is carried out by only 25 countries, the top 100 blue economy firms account for 60% of gross revenues generated from exploiting our oceans, and 97% of marine genetic resources have been patented by multinational enterprises in 10 rich countries. Although some progress has been made with regards to sustainable development of our oceans under the banner of the blue economy, only about 2% of countries worldwide appear to be on track to meet the targets under UN SDG#14 by 2030.

Conceptualizing the relationships between the blue economy, blue governance and blue justice remains challenging; however, understanding how they interplay together is essential for achieving a sustainable, equitable and just blue commons. This can in turn revitalize and advance existing business-society debates linked to ethics and social justice, helping to address some of the societal grand challenges.

The blue economy represents at least US$24 trillion in economic assets and generates around US$3 trillion in economic value annually, set to double by 2030. This makes it the seventh largest economy globally. In terms of sectoral coverage, it covers fishing and aquaculture, deep-sea mining and energy production, shipping, transportation, tourism and, sometimes, even national defence. The multisector nature of the blue economy makes it a particularly fruitful research area for exploring multi- and cross-sectoral approaches on how to address grand societal challenges against a particular environmental materiality, transnationality and aterritoriality.

Blue governance is a blue economy derivative from the general governance concept. It functions more as an umbrella concept covering a range of governance approaches linked to coastal governance, marine governance and ocean governance at local, national and supranational levels. It spans various sectors from fish and aquaculture species to seabed minerals, energy and tourism. As governance spaces, our oceans are highly contested because of the high economic, ecological, and strategic value of their resources. From a business-society perspective, the idea of blue governance extends beyond just spatial reach; it highlights a holistic and integrated approach to blue spaces and resources, focusing on plural knowledge, values, principles, identities, securities, in addition to the connectivity of marine species and human activities.

Examining how businesses, states, and civil society interact offers an important way to reassess assumptions about responsibilities, power, and coordination among actors engaged in transnational governance. The transnational and aterritorial nature of ocean contexts, along with their particular environmental materiality, offer a fruitful avenue for exploring the relationship between statehood and governance, which is especially interesting from the perspective of limited or diminished statehood in some emerging and developing countries and overseas territories. In such contexts, powerful non-state actors often emerge and fill the governance void. Firms, particularly multinational enterprises, often take on strong political roles, either in the pursuit of their interests or to fill the void in the governance of global public goods.

Exploring blue governance also offers an opportunity to problematize the ineffectiveness and deficiencies of Western governance approaches and philosophies in non-Western and indigenous contexts. There is a need to decolonize field structures, create hybrid institutional logics and diversify actor agency as particularities of indigenous contexts under limited statehood conditions, which are specifically linked to the exploitation of natural resources. Even where ocean-based initiatives contribute to sustainable development and are supported by effective forms of transnational governance, important social risks and inequities often still remain and require attention.

Compared to the blue economy and blue governance, the blue justice concept is a much younger concept. It serves as a normative benchmark between political actors and other stakeholder groups, and is underpinned by distributive, procedural, recognitional and restorative justice principles. The most comprehensive typology of blue justice issues includes: dispossession, displacement and ocean grabbing; waste and pollution environmental injustices; environmental degradation and erosion of environmental ecosystem goods; livelihood impacts for small-scale fisheries; access to marine resources supporting livelihoods and wellbeing; inequitable distribution of socio-economic benefits; social and cultural threats; marginalization of women and minorities; human and indigenous rights' abuses; and governance exclusion.

The aim of this Special Issue is to encourage cross-disciplinary research that examines oceans as a business–society nexus. It focuses on how blue economy activities interact with governance arrangements and social justice considerations, and how such interactions shape the economic, social, and ecological dimensions of ocean use. We welcome contributions that examine business–society relations in contexts related to oceans and coastal environments. Submissions may be empirical, conceptual, or review-based, including case studies at country, sectoral, or firm level, provided they move beyond description to generate broader insights into business–society dynamics in these settings.

We particularly welcome work that takes ocean- and coast-related phenomena as its starting point and reflects on how insights from these contexts inform existing debates in business-society research and beyond. Research involving human participants should be conducted with appropriate sensitivity to local contexts and research practices, including culturally appropriate methods and meaningful engagement with local communities. Indigenous-centered submissions should reflect relational ontologies and worldviews in which relationships among humans, non-humans, ancestors, and the land are constitutive of identity, and should honor indigenous ways of knowing and being, empower collective indigenous agency, benefit indigenous communities and advance indigenous rights.

The Special Issue also encourages submissions that engage with perspectives and regions that have been underrepresented in business and management research. This includes coastal and Indigenous communities and scholars based in the Small Pacific Island Nations, Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean. Contributions may examine how economic, social, and environmental considerations intersect in ocean- and coast-related contexts, including the trade-offs and tensions that arise between climate-related concerns and other sustainability challenges, and how these shape interactions between business actors, societal stakeholders, and governance arrangements in practice.

metaTitle: Please see Organizational Psychology Reviews current Call for Papers, Artificial Intelligence at Work and Organizational Psychology: Are
title: Artificial Intelligence at Work and Organizational Psychology: Are Our Theories Ready?
topics: How does AI impact the workplace and the people who work there? (this can take a multilevel perspective)
What are the implications of working with AI for group interactions, leadership (e.g. managerial decision making, leading teams), etc.?
How does AI impact the boundaries between work and nonwork activity?
What are the implications of AI for employee psychological and physical well-being?
What are and how can we develop ethical frameworks for research in AI that apply to the workplace?
How important is context in the implementation of AI and its effects on work?

How can we better understand issues related to levels of control we give to AI? Is AI a tool that augments work, or an autonomous teammate? Questions around agency, autonomy, and work design are also relevant.

How does the integration of AI affect negotiations in the workplace? How does existing theory about negotiations help us understand the issues in negotiation with an AI-driven team member? What about the case where the AI refuses to comply with a directive from a human?
What are theory-driven methodological considerations in considering AI's workplace impact?

Broadly, what does AI mean for theory and theory building in Organizational Psychology? AI itself is a phenomenon. How do we use theory to account for this phenomenon (if this is the right question?). Does our theory base account for specific AI driven phenomena (e.g., topics above like negotiating with AI, health effects of AI, leadership, and AI…)?

How can AI help with "new ways of seeing" in Organizational Psychology and related fields? How does existing theory have to change to account for AI? How can we get insights for our theories and concepts in Organizational Psychology and related fields from other disciplines (e.g. Information Systems)?

paragraphs: Artificial Intelligence has a significant and steadily growing impact on work, affecting employees, leaders in organizations, and researchers. This has been particularly striking since the advent of generative AI such as ChatGPT, a large language model AI system that can make fairly accurate predictions from vast amounts of data and engage in dialogue in a human-like manner to help solve complex problems.

Researchers are responding to rapid developments in AI as reflected in a surge of papers published in Organizational Psychology, Organizational Behavior, and Management that discuss the use of AI in personnel selection, implications of automation for work design, employee experience and engagement, coping with job insecurity when faced with automation, the impact of AI on group and team processes, leadership, developing causal models in leadership research, AI and workplace outcomes, and using generative AI in human resource management.

Several special issues and review papers focusing on AI highlight the need for research and theory building. Given the rapid developments in AI and expansion of its role at work, pertinent questions emerge: Are current theories fit for purpose? Are our theories ready to help us understand the AI revolution at work? If they are not adequate, do we need new theories to develop a coherent evidence base and explanations to understand how we can work with AI now and in the future? What are the limitations of AI as it augments work and what are possible ethical issues connected to it? Such questions suggest that good theory is critical for both driving science and enabling practice in organizations.

A few scholars have started to theorize about specific issues of working with AI and to evaluate how current theories are applicable to future work scenarios. These efforts highlight the importance of interdisciplinary perspectives in research on AI and the fact that literature streams in different subject areas explore similar questions from distinct angles but remain largely unconnected.

The purpose of this special issue is to shed light on what the implementation of AI in the workplace means for theory in Work and Organizational Psychology and related fields. This involves critically reviewing existing theories in the literature, revising and building new theories that account for the influence of AI in order to sketch out avenues for future research. The special issue seeks to understand where and how existing theories come up short in explaining processes and phenomena related to AI in the workplace, and whether there are concepts and constructs that need to be revisited, redefined, or newly developed.

Original conceptual papers, conceptual review papers, and meta-analyses are invited that contribute to theoretical understanding of AI in Organizational Psychology and related fields. Papers that integrate interdisciplinary perspectives are welcomed, with the expectation that Organizational Psychology and related fields will be a conceptual anchor in manuscripts that integrate or draw upon multiple perspectives. The emphasis of successful submissions will center on conceptual work, not on specific research or technical questions in AI.

metaTitle: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
title: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
topics: The 33 most cited entrepreneurship studies (each exceeding 1,000 citations) identified as priority candidates for replication
Influential studies within specific BCERC research tracks highlighted as influential contributions within each track
Studies with credible cases for broader influence on entrepreneurship research
Identifying boundary conditions and contextual contingencies of established relationships
Clarifying inconsistencies or mixed findings in prior research
Refining theoretical mechanisms underlying key constructs and relationships
Contributing to methodological transparency, rigor, and best practices in replication research
Multi-study designs combining exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension

paragraphs: This Special Issue seeks to advance our understanding of replication in entrepreneurship research by encouraging rigorous reexaminations of foundational empirical studies. Replication is essential for cumulative theory development and for establishing confidence in empirical findings. In a dynamic field such as entrepreneurship, where institutional environments, technologies, funding regimes, and societal expectations evolve rapidly, systematic replication is particularly critical to assess whether foundational relationships reflect stable theoretical mechanisms or context-specific patterns.

Despite its importance, recent evidence suggests that entrepreneurship research has not yet developed a strong replication culture. A comprehensive review shows that replication efforts remain rare, fragmented, and skewed toward conceptual extensions and empirical generalizations, while exact replications, reanalyses of original data, and checking-of-analysis designs are comparatively scarce. Moreover, many of the field's most influential empirical studies, particularly those published in leading journals and widely cited, have either never been replicated or have been replicated only once. As a result, widely cited findings continue to shape theoretical debates and inform practice without systematic assessment of their robustness, temporal stability, or boundary conditions.

This Special Issue calls for rigorous, theory-driven replication studies that revisit foundational relationships and contribute to a more robust and context-sensitive understanding of entrepreneurship phenomena. Replication is not viewed merely as a confirmation exercise but as a critical tool for theory refinement, extension, and adjudication between competing explanations. Submissions employing diverse methodological approaches are welcome, provided they are theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous. Multi-study designs that combine exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension are particularly encouraged, as such designs can offer deeper insights into when, how, and why established findings hold or vary across contexts.

All manuscripts will be subject to the journal's standard double-blind review process and must meet the publication standards of Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Submissions will be assessed based on their theoretical contribution, methodological rigor, and their ability to advance cumulative theory development in entrepreneurship, rather than on whether findings confirm prior results.

The guest editors will organize a series of paper development workshops (PDWs) aligned with the theme of the Special Issue prior to the submission deadline. The in-person workshop will take place at the University of North Texas in late February 2027, complemented by a virtual workshop in early March 2027. The PDWs are designed to support authors in developing rigorous, theory-driven replication studies, with particular encouragement for multi-study designs. Participation is entirely voluntary and is not a prerequisite for submission or consideration in the review process.

paragraphs: While society increasingly grapples with pressing social and environmental challenges, trust in modern-day capitalism is eroding. There has been a surge in interest among management and business and society researchers in cooperatives as a promising and influential alternative form of organizing. Cooperatives can help reduce inequality, safeguard workers' interests, confer greater control to members over their personal data, contribute to organizational resilience, and foster more responsible consumption. Cooperatives are expected to operate according to a set of cooperative principles promoted by the International Cooperative Alliance, which include autonomy and independence, cooperation among cooperatives, and democratic member control. Adherence to these principles underpins many of the benefits of cooperatives.

Democratic member control is perhaps the central feature distinguishing cooperatives from conventional enterprises. In addition to owning their cooperatives, members have the right and responsibility to effectively control them and shape their destiny, usually based on the principle of one member, one vote. However, cooperatives often find it challenging to implement and sustain democratic member control in practice. Cooperatives may be exposed to governance failures if they do not adapt their governance practices. Key sites of democratic participation in cooperatives like general assemblies and boards of directors often succumb to problems like low and unequal levels of member participation. Cooperatives have historically struggled with coordinating member participation in governance when they seek to operate beyond a local scale or when their membership base is heterogeneous, such as in multi-stakeholder cooperatives. Inadequate education and training about the importance of democratic member control has also compromised the ability of cooperatives to sustain participation. As such, the search for innovative approaches to cooperative governance matters more than ever.

Cooperatives have long been at the forefront of developing and experimenting with novel practices to improve and sustain their democratic governance. As laboratories for social innovation, cooperatives have long implemented innovative governance practices like providing women with voting and eligibility rights, enabling proportional voting, and promoting the formation of member councils. However, there is much room to expand our understanding of these and other innovations. The growth of the platform economy and corresponding rise of platform cooperatives and data cooperatives opens opportunities for new approaches towards the governance of cooperatives, including by means of technologies such as blockchain. However, these new types of cooperatives also generate unprecedented challenges, such as the potentially immense geographical spread of members, coming to terms with the use of complex emerging technologies, and balancing the interests of members and non-member investors.

Expanding our understanding of governance innovations in cooperatives will not only help cooperatives address the abovementioned challenges and achieve their social and environmental objectives, but can also serve as a powerful source of inspiration for burgeoning efforts to democratize conventional enterprises. This special issue seeks to synthesize existing knowledge and generate new insights about innovative approaches to the governance of cooperatives centered on four key themes: the application of new theories of democracy and governance to the governance of cooperatives; the inputs and processes underpinning governance innovations in cooperatives, including the use of new and emerging technologies for such innovations; the multi-layered, intended, and unintended outcomes of governance innovations in cooperatives; and the diffusion of governance innovations among cooperatives and other organizations.

Prospective authors are welcome to consider salient research questions spanning these themes as long as they fit within the research theme broadly and contribute to advancing our understanding of the field of business and society. The special issue particularly welcomes submissions that adopt an interdisciplinary approach and reflect the diversity of cooperative enterprises around the world. Conceptual and empirical papers using a variety of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods are all welcome as long as they meet the journal's standards for quality and rigour.

metaTitle: Strategy and Aesthetics
title: Strategy and Aesthetics
topics: The aesthetic qualities of strategy work: combining creative expression with analytical rigor; the coexistence of, and interplay between, poetics and reason
Aesthetically-infused experiences such as awe in understanding how strategic organizations resist the disenchantment of strategy work through over-rationalization

Studies of strategy confronting cultural landscapes encouraging the production and consumption of styles rather than goods, posing complex strategic identity choices across audiences with different stylistic preferences and evaluation criteria
How the strategic organization of affective forces is often caught in a fundamental ambiguity between instrumental organization and unmanageable reorganization of experience
Examinations of analogue and digital strategic devices and how these contribute to the performance of strategic styles, including strategy work in boardrooms and informal organizing contexts
Investigations of the strategic appropriation of artistic activity and how organizations draw from artistic practices to reinvent themselves and maximize profitability

Inquiries of processual forming and formation in strategy, invoking vitalist and new materialist philosophy and questions about organizational forms
Engagements with the raw material of strategy in formation, including how information and data have aesthetic forms and dimensions
Connecting strategy and temporality through aesthetics, including how strategy forms narrative plots that elicit specific feelings of progression, symbolic and communal attachments, and identities

paragraphs: There is broad recognition that organizational life cannot be fully understood or managed through rationalist frameworks. Scholars across the social sciences, including human geography and cultural theory, have long acknowledged how sensory experience, emotion, affect and embodied practice shape organization. Strategy studies are also beginning to understand how strategically significant phenomena–organizational routines, capabilities and identity, investment allocation and judgment, leadership, environmental adaptation–refuse to be confined to, and by, rational, logically structured analyses.

There is an aesthetic aspect to all strategy–it is as much vision as it reason; as much inspiration as analysis. Emotions, feelings, intuitions, desires and instincts can all have strategically significant influence. The symbolic and material dimensions of organising, alongside questions of purpose and structure across multiple human practices and fields, are all factors for which a successful strategic design must take account. The discursive, ecological and commercial forces to which organizations are adapting continually are encountered in aesthetic terms.

Organization theory is responding to this realization across multiple converging developments: the rise of design thinking and innovation discourse that foregrounds creative and experiential dimensions of value creation; growing attention to materiality and the physical environments in which work unfolds; and post-representational approaches that emphasize how knowing and organizing occur through sensory engagement rather than abstract cognition. From studies of organizational atmospheres and architectural spaces to analyses of craft work, branding practices, and the aesthetics of routine organizational artifacts, this scholarship has illuminated how aesthetic dimensions permeate organizational phenomena that were previously understood primarily through functional or instrumental lenses.

Despite this flourishing interest, explicit engagement with aesthetics in relation to strategy and strategic management has, for the most part, remained surprisingly limited. Aesthetically-minded scholars have examined topics adjacent to strategy, such as organizational identity, sensemaking, and innovation, with the strategic imperative toward creativity, or with questions of strategic fit and evolution. However, they have rarely focused explicitly on these being aesthetic considerations and experiences which are shaping the emergence and execution of organizational strategies. Conversely, mainstream strategy research has largely maintained its traditional emphasis on analytical frameworks, resource configurations, and performance metrics, with aesthetic dimensions remaining largely implicit or unexamined.

Contributing to this mutual neglect may be an underlying assumption that strategy and aesthetics are, to some degree, incompatible: strategy is typically associated with rational planning and directing, while aesthetic experiences are commonly viewed as detached from practical concerns. This special issue is dedicated to addressing this oversight, and to explicitly investigating the aesthetic aspects of strategic theory and practice. Strategy, we suggest, is grounded in aesthetics in a number of ways that merit further exploration.

paragraphs: Caste is a hierarchical division of society into different rungs, where the social, cultural, and economic rights and opportunities available to individuals are inherited at birth and not determined by their abilities. Caste affects how economic activity is organized, participation in it, and its outcomes for individuals, organizations, and societies in significant ways. This special issue studies the role and influence of caste in business and society as a field.

Caste derives its legitimacy from sub-continental scriptures that organize society into four immutable varnas or classes, and comprises thousands of jatis or smaller, occupation-based communities that one is born into. As an endogamous system, it traps individuals within their caste group and status and ensures that those at the bottom have limited socioeconomic mobility. Although commonly associated with Hinduism, caste operates across religious lines including Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism, and is widely observed in the South Asian sub-continent and further afield among the diaspora.

The globalization of supply chains means that caste is not restricted to South Asia alone but ought to be considered globally. Low-end and low-wage work in global supply chains is often undertaken by workers from marginalized caste groups. Furthermore, a 2020 lawsuit against Cisco for caste discrimination in California and the subsequent outlawing of caste-based discrimination in US cities and regions and universities demonstrate that caste deserves attention in terms of the wider circulation of commodities and labour in the global economy.

Caste creates imperfect, segmented, and monopolistic divisions in factor markets. It enables those belonging to dominant caste groups to appropriate both tangible and intangible resources while leaving marginalized caste groups with limited social and cultural capital and fewer professional and personal networks to leverage. This locks them out of available economic opportunities. As private economic activity continues to expand with limited regulation or protection for marginalized groups, caste-based inequalities are further embedded into the economy.

The enduring influence of caste-based divisions in society results in systematic exclusion of some castes from the market and leads to market failures as well as economic inefficiencies. In the absence of employment or entrepreneurial opportunities in the public and private sectors, workers from marginalized castes often turn to self-employment, micro-entrepreneurship, and wage work in the informal economy. In unregulated markets, dominant castes are able to hoard opportunities while continuing to subject marginalized castes to violence and impoverishment.

As a rigid hierarchy, caste directs occupational choices, more so for those trapped in its lower rungs. Dalits are often consigned to stigmatized or 'dirty work' such as scavenging, cleaning and sanitary work, in tanneries, and working with carcasses and corpses. Such low-wage, dangerous, and 'dirty work' leads to poverty, injuries to bodies and dignities, and exacerbates inequalities in society. Outside the caste-based occupational structure, caste continues to moderate employees' perceptions and outcomes of the labour market in significant ways.

Studies have found that Dalits continue to labour in precarious conditions, including modern slavery. Others have found that SC/ST workers face a 15 percent wage penalty, which is even more acute in private sector employment and can be directly attributed to caste-based discrimination. The possibility of future discrimination dampens Dalit students' expectations from the labour market, leading them to expect lower salaries and prefer public-sector jobs. This is unsurprising given homophily in private-sector enterprises among those owned by dominant castes, who are less likely to employ SC/ST workers.

Scholars have found caste homophily in decisions and interactions ranging from network formation, information sharing, and director/CEO hiring. Global production and supply chains replicate or reconfigure the role and influence of caste in economic activities. Some research has found that globalization and marketization has opened space for Dalit producers to participate in economic activities. In smallholder farming, the increase in wages has resulted in the exit of dominant caste farmers, while production has shifted to Dalit and other marginalized-caste smallholder farmers.

Given caste's enduring influence, entrepreneurship might appear a viable option as it promises autonomy for marginalized castes. However, studies have found that caste restricts entrepreneurialism and is socially unacceptable for them to start businesses. As a result, Dalit entrepreneurs often partner with dominant caste counterparts to facilitate access to resources. Caste moderates the organization, access to finance, and outcomes of entrepreneurial activities. MSMEs owned by individuals from socially marginalized backgrounds find it difficult to access institutional credit and encounter discrimination in loan amounts sanctioned, including in micro-credit on which the poor rely disproportionately.

Although largely concentrated in South Asia, caste's influence is by no means restricted to it. Recent work has theorized that caste's influence ranges from weak to moderate in global operations of Indian and non-Indian MNEs, making it far from redundant outside South Asia. Caste is known to influence social and economic relationships among the South Asian diaspora, with documented discrimination, exclusion, and microaggressions faced by Dalits in workplaces and social settings in various countries. However, the wider and more persistent presence of caste globally is evident through the rise of contracting and outsourcing in global supply chains, where caste exerts influence on the production of commodities and services in South Asia even when consumed outside it.

Even within modern professions, members from marginalized castes are frequently stigmatized and discriminated against. Despite equal qualifications, they are often assigned lower-skilled jobs and excluded from opportunities requiring more skills and competencies. Organizations essentialize and reproduce caste-based identities and stereotypes and fail to afford opportunities for further mobility. It is important to study not only how caste disadvantages marginalized castes but also the privileges it endows and how these are sustained among dominant castes.

Caste and caste-based networks endow social and cultural capital that enable individuals from dominant castes to create and access market opportunities. The hegemony of dominant castes in elite professions and positions has been widely noted, including on firms' boards and among firms' owners. Studies of CEO selection have found that recruiters prefer candidates with similar caste backgrounds as those of firms' owners and leaders. This hegemonic control over elite professions can also be seen inside business schools. Caste-based privileges are more enduring and invisibly transmitted across generations, which need to be studied in greater depth. Despite its endurance, caste remains relatively absent from large scholarship on business and society and related fields, and this absence merits further investigation.

There is a large body of evidence attesting to caste's impact on businesses and their activities and outcomes, but far less knowledge about what businesses and other organizations can do to tackle caste. While public sector organizations in India follow constitutionally-mandated reservations, the private sector does not have any such specific provisions or even caste-specific employee grievance mechanisms and practices. The role of businesses in expanding employment opportunities for marginalized castes has been limited.

There are no studies on how caste moderates firms' CSR behaviour and its effects. However, caste has affected businesses' philanthropy, with business leaders considering caste in social reform agendas from the early twentieth century, though remaining markedly circumscribed with focus on symbolic reform such as temple entry while leaving the wider caste system intact. Emergent scholarship has noted how caste impedes the functioning of social entrepreneurs such as development NGOs, with potential backlash from dominant castes over access to and sharing of resources and services. The fear of retaliation also prevents farmers from marginalized castes from sharing knowledge with other social intermediaries.

In addition to studying caste as a phenomenon, submissions using caste as a lens are welcome to evaluate and rethink theories relevant to business and society. Caste can be used to re-conceptualize theories in relation to agency, discrimination, diversity, inequalities, innovation, leadership, meritocracy, ownership and control over means of production, resistance, and stigma, among others. Such re-conceptualization on the specificities of caste as a social vector will make extant theories more comprehensive and relevant to the experiences of hundreds of millions of workers hitherto marginalized by the caste system globally.

paragraphs: This special issue seeks to explore the multifaceted ways in which political environments shape and influence the tourism and hospitality sectors. The political context encompasses governmental policies, political stability, regulatory frameworks, international relations, and geopolitical events that directly and indirectly affect tourism flows, hospitality operations, and industry development.

We invite submissions that examine how political factors influence destination competitiveness, tourism demand and supply, hospitality business strategies, employment patterns, and sustainable development in the sector. We particularly welcome research that addresses contemporary political challenges and opportunities in tourism and hospitality.

Contributions may include empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, case studies, and comparative analyses that provide insights into the complex relationships between political environments and tourism and hospitality industries globally.

paragraphs: The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Startups have a limited reputation as an employer which makes recruiting a challenge; however, there is evidence that talented individuals prefer startups in some contexts. As such, startups tend to recruit through previous affiliations and when proximal, these relationships can increase firm performance. Despite the allure of building a startup alongside founders and crafting unique roles, nascent firms have specific recruitment challenges and are generally more challenging places to work.

Startups tend to have underdeveloped human resources functions, leading to managerial and socio-structural challenges that ultimately trickle down to the employee. Scaling a startup's operations is difficult, and employees' growing pains are difficult to suppress during times of rapid expansion, leading to the accumulation of various forms of organizational 'debt' as the costs of growth outweigh the startup's ability to absorb them.

In sum, the startup context challenges traditional assumptions about employee-organization relationships, demanding new theoretical frameworks that can advance both entrepreneurship and organizational scholarship.

For the purposes of this special issue, the startup workforce is defined as the non-founding individuals who contribute labor to the creation and development of an early-stage venture. This workforce includes, but is not limited to, those under formal employment. As such, the workforce also encompasses contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost workers, and other non-standard labor that contributes to venture creation alongside payrolled employees. It is, however, distinct from founders and external stakeholders who do not work inside the venture. In practice, the boundary between the earliest employees and founders may be fuzzy, and contributions that interrogate how this boundary is drawn, contested, and made consequential are welcomed.

The special issue approaches the startup workforce as a relational phenomenon rather than a static population of employees inside a firm, one that spans individuals, firms, and the institutional environments in which startups are embedded. This framing invites contributions that take power, voice, and regulation seriously, and that use the distinctiveness of the startup context to export ideas back to adjacent fields.

This special issue aims to advance understanding of the startup workforce by bringing together researchers from fields such as entrepreneurship, organizational behavior, human resource management, economics, and sociology. Contributions from any disciplinary tradition are welcome, provided they engage substantively with the startup workforce. Theory borrowed from adjacent fields is welcome when it does genuine explanatory work for startup workforce phenomena; it is not welcome when it provides labels for statistical relationships without specifying the mechanisms through which those relationships operate in the entrepreneurial context.

Consistent with the journal's editorial direction, submissions are evaluated on the alignment between research question, research design, and data quality. An important research question about the startup workforce, paired with a design capable of answering it and data of sufficient quality to support credible conclusions, matters more than theoretical novelty or conceptual sophistication. The journal values work that not only explains mechanisms but also clarifies what the evidence means for the choices founders, employees, and investors face in practice.

Empirical papers that illuminate convincing causal mechanisms are highly encouraged, whether through quasi-experimental designs, longitudinal panel studies, field experiments, qualitative process tracing, ethnographies, or mixed-methods research. The journal is equally receptive to computational approaches and studies that leverage novel data sources: linked employer-employee datasets, platform data, administrative records, and other unconventional sources can open windows into startup employment dynamics. Multi-method approaches that triangulate findings across different research designs are especially valued.

For studies relying on distal sources such as archival or census data, authors are expected to demonstrate how the theorized mechanisms are reflected in the measurement architecture, not merely inferred. Data quality is evaluated by fitness-for-purpose rather than by representativeness alone, and work that invests in novel infrastructure and integrates multimodal sources is welcomed. Designs that exploit exogenous variation in the policy environment of startup employment, such as changes in non-compete enforcement, worker classification rules, equity-compensation taxation, or visa regimes, to identify causal effects on recruitment, retention, mobility, and venture outcomes are particularly welcome.

Given the nested nature of the startup workforce, multi-level theoretical approaches and research designs are appreciated; the interplay among individual employees, founder-employee dyads, teams, organizations, and broader labor markets represents fertile ground for contributions that capture the complexity of startup employment. Studies that pre-register hypotheses, share replication materials, or otherwise embrace open-science principles are valued and will be recognized during the review process. Direct and conceptual replications, robustness and multiverse analyses, informative null findings, and Registered Reports-style submissions with pre-reviewed designs are welcomed.

The rapid development of AI-based tools has fundamentally changed what it means to produce a conceptual contribution. Purely review-oriented papers and conceptual pieces that primarily synthesize existing ideas without empirical grounding are less likely to be competitive; however, field-defining theoretical contributions that advance understanding beyond what existing work has established will be considered.

paragraphs: Family firms continue to be an important domain of study in the organization sciences. In terms of numbers, family businesses represent a dominant form of economic organization throughout the world. Therefore, family business scholarship needs to generate generalizable theory across the spectrum of these heterogeneous organizations. Family business research is receiving attention from scholars across the globe, providing an increasing body of knowledge that still has many unanswered questions.

Scholars are invited to prepare 5-page abstracts examining and extending family business research utilizing a variety of theoretical perspectives. These perspectives include stewardship theory, stakeholder theory, property rights theory, agency theory, institutional theory, prospect theory, resource-based theory, justice theories, social exchange theory, family science theory, and network theory, all of which potentially have unexplored avenues that could inform our understanding of family enterprise. Likewise, family business as viewed from the broad conceptual lens of fields such as strategic management, entrepreneurship, organizational behavior, economics, psychology, and sociology should further contribute to this goal of integrating new theory with family firm research.

The submitted abstracts will be evaluated by the editorial team and select author(s) will be invited to submit full manuscripts based on their ideas to present at the in-person conference affiliated with this special issue. The goal of the special issue is to build theory specifically informing family businesses and their stakeholders which in turn could be utilized to develop theory for the broader organizational sciences.

Manuscripts submitted should not be review pieces, bibliometric analyses, meta-analyses, or other forms of knowledge accumulation or summary unless they clearly, specifically, and strongly develop novel theoretical insights that inform family firm theory. Works from macro, meso, and micro perspectives are welcomed, particularly those that attempt to develop theoretical insights that inform how family firms operate. Pieces that include strong empirical tests that apply theory in family firms and inform how family business issues are impacted by different theoretical issues are highly encouraged.

The Theories of Family Enterprise Conference is intended to bring a small number of the leading scholars from mainstream disciplines such as strategic management, organization theory, organizational behavior, finance, economics, and entrepreneurship together with leading scholars in family business management in order to explore theories, research, and interdisciplinary perspectives on family businesses. For each paper, the author team will receive feedback from conference participants to help them further illuminate and explore the contributions of their work. The conference aims to consist of 10-12 full manuscripts, making the submission and review process highly competitive.

Up to two authors from each selected paper will receive complimentary lodging and meals for three nights of the conference. All attendees are responsible for their own travel to/from the conference venue. The 2025 conference will be hosted by Florida State University and held at their campus in Florence, Italy. Conference participants will stay at the B&B HOTEL Florence Pitti Palace at the Ponte Vecchio in the historic downtown district of the city. Due to space constraints, the conference is limited only to authors of accepted papers. Additionally, authorship is limited to two submissions.
